XVII. GENDER BUDGETING
17.1 Gender Budgeting is a powerful tool for addressing gender based disparities and achieving
women empowerment through mainstreaming gender corners across sector. Gender budgeting
enables in maintaining a gender perspective at all stages, including formulation of policies and
schemes, allocation of policies and schemes, allocation of resources, implementation, monitoring
and review. It leads to translation of gender commitments into budgetary commitments.
17.2 A Plan Scheme for Gender Budgeting was launched in the year 2008 during the Eleventh
Plan period, for conducting, training/workshops, capacity building, research surveys etc. Under the
Scheme, inter alia , the Ministry undertakes many programmes as well as provides financial support
for the purpose. An outlay of `1.30 crore (at RE stage) was allocated for the Scheme in the year
2014-15, for conducting various training programmes and workshops on Gender Budgeting. Out of
which, an amount of `1.07 crore have been incurred till January, 2015. An amount `2.00 crore

33
(BE) has been allocated for the year 2015-16. The Committee notes that so far 57 Ministries/
Departments have set up Gender Budgeting Cells. A total of 18 States and 3 UTs have undertaken
various Gender Budgeting Initiatives.
17.3 The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Women and Child Development
being the nodal agency for gender budgeting should focus upon the proper allocation to and
full utilization of the Gender Budgeting Scheme. There has been a considerable progress
made in this area which have concerns across the Ministries both at the Central and State
level from the perspective of women specific schemes. The focus should be aimed at
strengthening and empowering the Gender Budgeting Cells to enable them to undertake
their envisaged role effectively.
17.4 Like Gender Budgeting, Child Budgeting can be considered another major initiative
in sensitizing and institutionalizing child-related concerns. For this purpose, the Committee
notes that the Ministry will have to build capacities to analyse the Central and State
budgets and their impact on the betterment children.
XVIII. CONCLUSION
18.1 The Ministry of Women and Child Development was set up as a nodal agency with
the prime aim to empower and promote holistic development and welfare of women and
children who are considered the vulnerable sections of society. The Ministry has formulated
many women and child centred legislations, plans, policies and programmes to ensure
women’s empowerment as well as gender equality to the extent possible and to ensure
children’s holistic development and growth. The Committee is aware that the Ministry has
to cater to more than 70 per cent of the total population and that too the most vulnerable
ones. It, therefore, has indeed a massive responsibility. The Committee finds the
performance of the Ministry satisfactory but still a lot more needs to be done, particularly
for arresting the rising crimes against women and children. The Committee strongly feels
that the Ministry should ensure safety and security to women including at the workplace,
by ending all forms of discrimination, exploitation, harassment and violence against women
by strictly implementing the relevant laws promulgated for the purpose. Further, the
Ministry should strive towards ensuring zero tolerance to all kinds of exploitation of
children including child labour, sexual abuse and violence, by providing legislative and
institutional support. The Committee is of the view that the Ministry would find it very
difficult to fulfill the objectives of empowerment of women in all walks of life due to
massive cut in funds this year. The Committee also feels that it should have better
coordination with the State Governments and various agencies, NGOs for implementing
women/children centric schemes for more better results.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE — AT A GLANCE
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
The Committee is dismayed to note that there has been a substantial decrease in
budgetary allocation in child welfare schemes. The same is the case with the schemes
related to women also. Though the Finance Minister has announced in this year’s budgetary
speech (Para 55) that extra resources of around `1500 crores would be provided as
depending on additional resources. However, the Ministry seems to have been caught
unawares about such a massive budget cut. Devolution of funds to the States as per
recommendation of the Fourteenth Finance Commission is yet to concretize. Even if it
comes, the experience with States contributing their share had not been very encouraging.
So, with this budget cut, there is a question mark as to how and when these States would
contribute remaining part. Thus, the Ministry has been left in lurch affecting the very
implementation of the existing Schemes. The Committee, however, recommends that all out
efforts be made to see that the State Governments contribute their share as soon as
possible so that the projected targets can be achieved efficiently and in a timely manner.
The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of Finance should make `1500 crores as
promised by Minister of Finance before Parliament at the earliest lest the schemes of the
Department should suffer. (Para 2.3)
The Committee observes that in almost all the major schemes, except only one
scheme namely, National Commission for Women, BE allocation has been drastically brought
down at the RE stage. Further, it is unfortunate to note that in the major schemes, the
funds allocated have not been utilized to the fullest extent. Also in the scheme of National
Nutrition Mission, the utilization of funds is nil and for the scheme of One Stop Crisis
Centre, no fund had been allocated in the RE stage in the year 2014-15. The Committee
would like to point out that in major schemes like ICDS and SABLA, the funds allocated
in BE 2015-16 has been cut to great extent that the achieving the physical targets of these
schemes might have been affected.  This needs to be checked and the Committee desires
that a status note on this be furnished to the Committee for its consideration.  (Para 2.5)
The Committee observes from the reason given by the Ministry for non-utilization
that these social sector schemes were included in the Ministry’s budget in anticipation that
these would be approved for the implementation. But for 2 schemes out of 8, none could
be approved. Therefore, the budgetary allocation has not been utilized. It also appears to
be the main reason for reduction in allocations at RE stage during these years. The
Committee takes a serious view of such an approach on the part of the Ministry in this
regard and recommends that it should have made serious attempt to get all the approvals
for the implementation of the Schemes for better utilization of funds. (Para 2.7)
The Committee finds that the performance of the Scheme like SABLA has been
satisfactory, however for the IGMSY Scheme, the physical targets remained under-achieved
in 2013-14 and 2014-15. Schemes related for girl child, adolescent girls and women are of
vital importance, so any problems faced in the achievement of targets need to be identified
and addressed for the efficacious implementation of the schemes. (Para 2.9)
The Committee notes the concerted efforts made by the Ministry to liquidate the
pending UCs and the progress made so far. However, it would like to point out that in spite

of their efforts, there is still a good number of UCs that are pending. Consistent efforts on
the part of the Ministry are required for liquidation of the remaining UCs. Constraints
faced in the procedural formalities and accounting system need to be identified and
addressed so as to ensure compliance with all the prescribed requirements. The Committee
hopes that urgent steps on a priority basis would be taken by the Ministry to liquidate the
remaining UCs especially the old UCs and desires that a status note may be furnished to
the Committee at the earliest for its perusal and consideration. (Para 2.11)
It has been brought to the attention of the Committee that no internal audit of the
Ministry has been conducted after 2007 . The Committee is constrained to observe that for
such an important Ministry catering to about 70  per cent of the population, a systematic and
regular mechanism for auditing is not put in place. The Committee would like to point out
that internal auditing is necessary to add value and improve an organization’s operations.
So it is hoped that internal auditing is done regularly so that the Ministry can accomplish
its objectives. (Para 2.12)
III.  HIGHLIGHTS OF WORKING GROUP REPORT ON CHILD RIGHTS
Keeping in view of the present position of children in the country, the Committee
believes that efforts are required to ensure that resources are judiciously utilized towards
implementing new schemes and that right preparations should be made for a better and
efficient implementation of these Schemes. There is a need for efforts to provide flexibility
of norms to address critical needs at the community level by creating a flexi-pool of
resources and the need for funding schemes with realistic cost norms. Policy formulation,
strengthening programmes execution, enforcement of laws, plan implementation, capacity-
building and scheme monitoring are some of the areas that need immediate attention and
strengthening. Convergence between various sectoral policies and programmes that impact
the lives of children and inter-sectoral coordination are vital for bridging the shortfalls in
achievements. (Para 3.3)
IV. INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES SCHEME (ICDS)
The Committee notes that there has been a consistent increase in the allocations over
the last three years, except for the current year of 2015-16 where the allocation has been
reduced substantially to `8335.77.  T he ICDS Scheme is the biggest and most unique
programme. The Committee, however, observes that budget cut this year is in total contrast to
the significance of the Scheme. There will be difficulty in meeting the expenses of the targets
laid down by the Ministry, though the Finance Minister has promised additional funds. The
Ministry expressed its serious concern regarding the budget cut and did not have a back-up plan
to cover these expenses. All hope lies with the States that they will contribute their share. But
this is doubtful that it will be done in time observing the past trend of the performances of
States/UTs in contributing their share towards meeting the expenses of the schemes. With an
amount of `17, 000 crores being devolved by the Centre to the States and also `2,85,000 crores
to urban local bodies, it is hoped that the national priorities laid down by the Government will
be followed by States/UTs. The Committee desires to know the extent these Schemes are likely
to be affected in case States does not follow Centre in this regard. Instant arrangement be
made for the allocation announced by the Finance Minister. (Para 4.5)
Status of Infrastructure in Anganwadi Centres
The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry in trying to fulfill its financial
and physical targets. However, a lot more can be done to fill the gap in making sanctioned

36
AWCs operational. The Committee feels that the constraints that develop in the process
should be identified and taken care of. (Para 4.7)
The Committee observes that in terms of toilet facilities in A WCs, barring a few
States like Nagaland, Uttrakhand and UTs like Chandigarh, Delhi, Daman and Diu and
Lakshadweep, almost all the States have a long way to go to achieve this target. This is a
sad situation, when the Hon’ble Prime Minister of this Nation is spreading the Swachh
Bharat Abhiyan to every nook and corner of the country, the AWCs are not being provided
with the most basic of facilities like drinking water and toilets. The Committee would like
to point out that the Ministry should identify the hurdles that came up in this process and
should be dealt with earnestly. (Para 4.13)
World Bank assisted ICDS Systems Strengthening and Nutrition Project (ISSNIP)
The Committee feels that nothing much has been done for a project which was
launched on 9
th May, 2013. The time period of the Phase 1 of the project is coming to a
close, yet no achievements have been made so far. For such an important scheme, steps
should be taken up by the Ministry so that effective results are brought about by the proper
implementation of the Scheme. (Para 4.16)
Pre-School Education (PSE) Kit and Medicine Kits
The Committee would like to point out the importance of the PSE and Medicine kits
in AWCs which introduce the young children to non-formal pre-school education through a
variety of activities and teaching and provide them medical aid whenever required during
their stay in an AWC. It was also to facilitate the transition of the pre-school children in
AWCs to the primary school. The Committee desires that proper care and attention may be
shown while implementing the Schemes. (Para 4.19)
Staff and Key Functionaries of ICDS
The Committee would like to emphasize that the problem of vacant positions of key
ICDS functionaries - AWHs, Supervisors and CDPOs continues to persist which adversely
affect the delivery of services in an A WC. With the expansion and strengthening of ICDS
Scheme, a lot more efforts need to be made in order to fill the vacancies. The Committee
was made to understand that the Ministry has been trying to reduce the vacancy position.
ICDS functionaries play a vital role in the functioning of the various ICDS Scheme. So, for
every scheme to achieve its targets/goals and to function efficiently, the vacancy problem
that continues for a long time needs to be addressed as soon as possible.  The Committee
also observes that Anganwadi Workers must be remunerated adequately properly so that
they are motivated to perform their requisite tasks. (Para 4.21)
The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry in increasing the
remuneration paid to Anganwadi Workers and also other benefits given to them but feels
that they are still on the lower side and require upward revision for better implementation
of the Schemes. The Committee further points out that there seems to be no pension
scheme for the A WWs/AWHs. It is to be understood that the AWWs are the most crucial
functionary of ICDS Scheme. The Committee, therefore, would like to again emphasize that
the presence of a committed cadre of these functionaries is an important tool for successful
implementation of any scheme. (Para 4.24)
The Committee would like to emphasize that awards work as incentives for boosting
the morale of workers and making them more involved in their official responsibilities.

37
Delay in awarding the worker for more than 5 years can only be considered as making a
mockery of principle of giving incentives by any organization. The Committee accordingly,
recommends that the selection process should be completed without any further delay and
services of deserving functionaries be duly recognized. (Para 4.26)
The Committee takes note of the various findings of the study and suggests that
more initiatives should be taken to improve the programme implementation. The Ministry
should innovate new ways to tackle malnutrition, for example, use of technology to identify
and monitor malnutrition among children, improving the quality of Take Home Rations, etc.
(Para 4.28)
V. INTEGRATED CHILD PROTECTION SCHEME (ICPS)
The Committee observed from the above table that all the States and UTs have
signed the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) under the ICPS Scheme, the last being
Telangana on 20
th October, 2014 . The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry
in its effort to implement the Scheme in all the States. The ICPS Scheme has finally picked
up with increasing utilization of allocated funds and increasing number of beneficiaries
except the year 2013-14. The Committee also notes that there was a sharp decline in
allocation for the Scheme as against the projected demand. ICPS is a scheme which is of
immense importance for the protection of children. For the proper implementation of such
an important scheme, adequate funds should be allocated. The Committee feels that the
Ministry should approach the Government for allotment of enough funds. Also, the States/
UTs should devise an effective and efficient delivery structures and recruit enough staffs so
that the scheme is implemented properly. The Committee believes that ICPS is the scheme
for spreading a wide protective network of structures for helping distressed children in need
of care. The Scheme should be taken more seriously and the Ministry would have to play
a pro-active role in this regard. The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should take
the implementation aspect of the scheme with the State Governments/UTs and regularly
monitor the progress of the Scheme . Further, the State Government/UT Administrations
need to be sensitized and training of staff should be emphasized upon for successful
implementation of the Scheme. (Para 5.4)
Inspection of Homes
The Committee would like to express its satisfaction over the various steps taken to
deal with the issue of sexual abuse of children. The Committee welcomes the positive steps
taken by the Ministry in coordination with other concerned agencies and the State
Governments/UT Administrations. The need of the hour is the proper implementation of the
various provisions laid down in the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act,
2000. It is also important that the States/UTs make an effort to implement the Act to
punish the perpetrators and also to prevent further committing of crimes. Moreover, the
Committee feels that public at large needs to be made aware of these legal provisions and
facilities available to the victims so that committing of any such crimes be prevented and
justice be served. (Para 5.17)
VI. BETI BACHAO BETI PADHAO (BBBP) PROGRAMME
The Committee observes that the steadily declining child sex ratio in India has
reached emergency proportions and urgent action must be taken to alleviate this crisis. The
Committee further observes that this decline has taken place despite the best efforts by the
Ministry in checking this trend. It should be noted that girl child is the future of every

38
nation and India is no exception. In a society, both girls and boys, play equally important
roles. To eliminate girl child from the society is a step backward, away from the civilized
society. So, for the society and the nation as a whole to grow and progress, the girl child
must be saved, cared, nurtured and loved. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Ministry should make all out efforts to check this declining CSR in a mission mode and
also to put more aggressiveness, energy and resources to reverse this trend. (Para 6.3)

structures for service delivery to maximum pregnant and nursing women requiring cash
incentives for their health, nutrition and also partial compensation for their wage loss.

the stakeholders involved directly or indirectly for the protection and rehabilitation of

understand that a number of capacity building programmes have been conducted by CARA
for the various stakeholders at the State level to sensitize them on the advantages of early

Information & Guidance System) - an IT application introduced by CARA for greater
transparency in the adoption system. Continuous promotional efforts and enhanced

With Andaman and Nicobar Islands as exception, the Committee observes that in all
the States/UTs, the amount of loan disbursed to poor women was less than the sanctioned
amount indicating that funds are lying un-utilized with IMOs in these States. The
Committee is dismayed with the findings that in certain States like Karnataka and Punjab,
less than half of the sanctioned amount was being disbursed. The same situation prevails
in the UT of Puducherry in which funds amounting to only `16 crore is being disbursed
since inception against a sanctioned amount of `51 crore. A major discrepancy observed by
the Committee is the number of beneficiaries vis-à-vis  loans disbursed. In the State of
Assam e.g. against `453.90 lakh disbursed, there were only 6605 beneficiaries. The same can
be said for the State of Bihar where `468.83 lakh benefitted 17,156 women. The Committee
notes this issue and strongly feels that a monitoring mechanism should be put in place to
curtail any discrepancy that arises in the whole process. Also, the Committee feels that the
fund sanctioned should be duly disbursed without any delay as this Scheme aims for the
economic empowerment of the poor women. (Para 10.4)
The Committee is happy to note the positive outcomes of the scheme of RMK which
has led to economic empowerment of poor women in the identified States as highlighted in
the impact assessment studies. Not just this, economic empowerment of these women also
resulted in increasing their self-confidence and awareness and has given them respect and
a say in decision making leading to their social empowerment. The Committee believes that
in order to sustain and increase the reach of the scheme to the targeted women, sustained
efforts need to be made by the Ministry to utilize the allocated funds and closely monitor
the progress of the Scheme. (Para 10.6)

The Committee feels that a lot more can be done for improving the performance of
the scheme with respect to construction of more hostels for working women. All the

REPORT
1. INTRODUCTION
Department of Sports is a Department under the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports.
Sports and Games have always been perceived as an integral component in the all-round
development of personality. Apart from being a means of entertainment and physical fitness, sports
have always played a greater role in generating spirit of healthy competition and bonding among
us. Today, sports emerge as an important component of socio-economic development of the
country and the Government plays a crucial role in promoting sports. The Government and
governmental organizations are responsible in making sports policies, allocating grants for
developing infrastructure, nurturing talents and designing specialized programmes for overall
development of sports.
2. Today, many types of sports are played across the country. Things apart, regional games
have also become a way of life. India first participated at the Summer Olympic Games in 1920,
and, since then, has participated in every Summer Olympic Games. India’s first achievement in
Gold Medal in Olympics dates back to the 1928 Summer Olympic Games, winning Men’s Field
Hockey. Abhinav Bindra became the first Indian to win an individual Gold Medal at the Olympic
Games.
3. India’s performance is disheartening among nations for having won very few Olympic
Medals, despite a population of over 1.2 billion. Several explanations, among others, have been
attributed for abysmal performance which inter alia includes poverty, mal-nutrition, neglected
infrastructure, lack of sponsorship, institutional disor ganization, etc. As regards Commonwealth
Games, India has competed in fourteen out of the eighteen previous Commonwealth Games. Since
the inception in 1934, India hosted the games once in 2010. India is fourth most successful
country with a total of 436 Medals including 156 Gold Medals.
4. The year 1982 is significant in the history of sports in India as India organized the IX Asian
Games in Delhi . Prior to that not much emphasis had been given towards sports in public policies.
National Sports Policy, 1984 was the first move towards developing an organized and systematic
framework for the development and promotion of sports in the country, and the precursor of the
present National Sports Policy, 2001. The twin planks of the National Sports Policy 2001 are
“Broad-basing of Sports” and “Achieving Excellence in Sports” at the national and international
levels. The salient features of the Policy are as:–
➢ Broad-basing of sports and achievement of excellence;
➢ Upgradation and development of infrastructure;
➢ Support to National Sports Federations and other sports bodies;
➢ Strengthening of scientific and coaching support to sports;
➢ Special incentives to promote sports;
➢ Enhanced participation of women, scheduled tribes and rural youth;
➢ Involvement of corporate sector in sports promotion; and
➢ Promote sports mindedness among the public at large.
5. With increased exposure to global sporting events, there is a growing market today for new
sports. The phenomenal rise in the youth population has made India youngest nation with a
demographic dividend appearing to be a reality. Undoubtedly, young Indians have found a whole

2
new set of sporting heroes. Adding to this, we find a slew of recent wins by Indian sporting icons
which have inspired youngsters to pursue their passion for sports. Based on these developments,
some evident and some latent, it is to be believed that the Indian sports is transcending through
significant changes.
6. The role of the government in the development of sports may be gauzed as threefold –
➢ The Government must allocate land and resources to develop sports facilities.
➢ The Government must create an environment that will allow the grassroot programmes
that are sprouting across the nation to flourish.
➢ All schools should support the initiatives taken by the Government and allocate sufficient
time and resources to physical fitness and sports activities.
Further the Department of Sports, inter alia deals with matters relating to broad-basing of
Sports, anti-doping, uses of sports stadia, etc.
7. The Secretary in his presentation before the Committee on the 17
th April, 2015 gave an
overview of the functioning and status of different schemes/programmes being executed by the
Department. He described that sports is a state subject and it is primarily the responsibility of the
State Governments to create adequate sports infrastructure within the States. Further, the Central
Government complements and supplements efforts of States in this regard. Nevertheless, the
Department of Sports, in the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, has two primary objectives. One
is broad-basing of sports, that is, of making sports available to all. So, in this context, there are
two major schemes running in the Department. First, which was earlier called as the Panchayat
Yuva Krida and Khel Abhiyan (PYKKA), has now been restructured into the Rajiv Gandhi Khel
Abhiyan (RGKA). Another one is the Urban Sports Infrastructure Scheme, which is for
development of sports infrastructure in the urban centres in the country. The issue regarding the
broad-basing of sports, strictly speaking is not with the Department, however, the efforts are to
encourage sports through the school system. Somehow, it is being transformed as a regular part
of the school curriculum because that is where the real identification, the development of sports
has to automatically come from. The other major objective of the department is in ‘achieving
excellence in sports’. And, in this context, there are two major areas. One is the National Sports
Federation (NSF), which has the responsibility of developing that particular game and also of
selecting the team at the national level, training, nominating the teams for participation in events
and tournaments abroad, and so on. NSFs are autonomous organizations and the Government has
no involvement in their day-to-day working. Second, of course, is the Sports Authority of India
(SAI). The Sports Authority of India has different schemes for identification and nurturing of talent
from the sub-junior level to the elite level. It is also responsible for the training of national teams.
8. The Committee was also apprised of some of the recent initiatives that have been
undertaken. The most important is that of setting of the Manipur Sports University in Manipur. This
was announced in the last year’s Union Budget. The Department is taking steps to get it
established. The site has been identified. The land is likely to be available soon. Second major
initiative, again announced in the last year’s Union Budget, was the National Sports Talent Search
Scheme (NSTSS), which basically deals with identification of sporting talent in the country in the
age group of 8-12 years. The scheme has been developed and notified and the initial selections
should be taking place in September-October this year. The third initiative is the setting up of
national academies in some of our major prominent sports, largely under the aegis of SAI in
collaboration with the National Sports Federations. The fourth is the development of sports
infrastructure in Jammu and Kashmir. This special initiative was announced by the Union Finance
Minister in the last year’s Budget. This basically involves remodeling and renewal of the two major
stadia in Srinagar and Jammu and also development of some sports facilities in district

3
headquarters. Moreover, the Department has two major initiatives which have been going on for
some time now, that is, the setting up of Indian Institute of Sports Science and Medicine and the
National Institute of Sports Coaching. These two projects are still at the formulation stage and will
take some more time for getting established.
9. The Committee was also informed that concerning the performance of individual nations in
medals tally at the Olympic Games, name of Cuba may be cited as an example. Considering that
Cuba’s population is only around 11 million (around half the size of New York metro area), Cuba
is the most successful Olympic team by total medals won. Cuba first participated at the Olympic
Games in 190 0, and had sent athletes to compete in 19 of 27 Summer Olympic Games overall.
Cuban athletes have won a total of 208 medals at the Summer Olympics. In modern Cuban society,
sports and physical education begin from childhood. Children are taught at a later age to play
games that resemble physical exercise. These ideas are the basis for the modern sports
programmes in Cuba, and clearly these are working.

12. In view of the winding up of the Planning Commission, which was an in intermediary

SPORTS AUTHORITY OF  INDIA (SAI)
13. The Sports Authority of India (SAI) is the field arm of the Department and was set up in
1984 as a registered Society. SAI is engaged in spotting and nurturing talent at all levels by
providing the requisite infrastructure and equipment, coaching facilities, scientific back up,
nutritious diet, competition and exposure. It is also entrusted with the responsibility of maintaining
and utilizing, on behalf of the Department, the five Stadia in Delhi which were constructed/
renovated for the IX Asian Games held in New Delhi in 1982.
14. There are 9 Regional Centres of SAI, which are located at Bangalore, Gandhinagar, Delhi,
Lucknow, Chandigarh, Kolkata, Imphal, Bhopal and Sonepat. In addition, through the Netaji
Subhash National Institute of Sports (NIS) Patiala, its academic arm, SAI offers a variety of
courses in sports coaching and sports medicine; and graduate and post-graduate courses in physical
education are offered at the Lakshmibai National College of Physical Education (LNCPE),
Thiruvananthapuram.
15. There are total of around 3000 employees in SAI including around 1200 coaches deployed
all over the country; a brief outline of schemes implemented by SAI for spotting and nurturing of
sports talent and the promotion of sports in the country is as under:–
➢ National Sports Talent Contest (NSTC)
➢ Army Boys Sports Companies (ABSC)
➢ Specail Area Games (SAG)
➢ SAI Training Centres (STC)
➢ Centres of Excellence (COE)

7

country. Reducing its allocation instead of increasing over the years does not augur well for
the development of sports in our country.
20. The Committee recommends that initiatives should be taken to fill up vacant posts
of Coaches urgently, required for every sports discipline and they get international training
and exposure regularly. The need for various levels of Coaches Education and Certification
System (CECS) structure, procedure for getting International Federations Certification, etc.
have to be adequately taken care of besides the initiatives required for filling up the

21. The Committee was given to understand that in Andhra Pradesh there is no dearth
of sports talents in archery, particularly in interior tribal areas. The Committee, therefore,

ASSISTANCE TO NATIONAL SPORTS FEDERATIONS
22. The Committee came to know that SAI through its Training of Elite Athletes and
Management Support (TEAMS) Division, provides support to National Sports Federations (NSFs)
by way of coordinating their Long Term Development Plans (LTDPs), and providing logistic and
training support. In this role, a number of activities are being carried out by SAI out of funds
provided to them by the Ministry.
23. The Department recognizes only one federation of each sport discipline at the national level.
The recognized National Sports Federation (NSF), in turn, is responsible for the promotion and
development of the sport. The NSF has to discharge the responsibilities in accordance with the
principles laid down in the Olympic Charter or in the Charter of Indian Olympic Association (IOA),
or the relevant International Federation. The Government only supplements the efforts of National
Sports Federation (NSFs) by providing financial assistance for participation in international events
abroad, conducting national/international tournaments and training/coaching of national teams under
Indian and Foreign Coaches/Experts, etc., under the Scheme of ‘Assistance to national Sports
Federations’. In all these matters, Sports Authority of India (SAI) closely coordinates with NSFs.
24. The Department regularly consults NSFs in major decision making, e.g., the NSFs were
consulted while formulating criteria for Sports Awards, revision of Schemes of the Department,
etc. The Department also either directly or through Sports Authority of India (SAI) consults the
NSFs while implementing its various schemes. The Ministry has evolved an evaluation/performance
monitoring mechanism of the NSFs. Government has also issued instructions to NSFs to
mandatorily declare information on their website pertaining to their audited accounts, balance sheet,
selection criteria for athletes, etc. by 1.4.2015.
25. The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that there is a distinct lack of proper
coordination and control mechanism among the NSFs on the one hand between the Ministry/
SAI and the NSFs on the other hand. The NSFs in the name of their autonomy, the
Committee feels, that they are not accountable to anybody even though they receive
Government funds for their activities. The NSFs, the Committee, feels have a definite role
to play in promoting different sports disciplines in the country. But their working leaves

8
much to be desired. These bodies, unfortunately, devote much of their time and resources
in the non-sporting activities. Most of them have not been able to live upto the
expectations. No doubt, some of them done or doing very good work in the promotion of
sports in the country. The Committee has been expressing its concern over this issue from
time to time and calls upon the Ministry and the representatives of the NSFs to find out
collectively a most efficient and workable solution that can bring our sports sector out of
the present situations. We may perhaps try to learn/adopt the best practices in this respect
from the other countries such as China, Korea, Taiwan, etc.
26. As regards non-compliance of the guidelines, by the NSFs, the Committee was apprised that
the Archery Association of India has been de-recognised since it refused to accept the Government
guidelines; the recognition of Indian Amateur Boxing Federation was suspended and subsequently
the same was not renewed. Recognition to Korfball Football Federation of India has not been
accorded recognition since 2012 for not accepting Government Guidelines. Gymnastics Federation
of India and Athletics Federation of India were asked to hold fresh elections which they have
complied with.
27. The Committee finds it very disheartening on the issue of non-compliance of the
guidelines of the Department by the NSFs and recommends to evolve a suitable mechanism
in this regard so that the preparation as well as participation of the sportspersons in
important national and international events is not affected adversely.

28. The Committee is at a loss to see that the audit observations made in the
Commonwealth Games, 2010 by the CAG have not been cleared so far. The Committee finds
it objectionable and desires the Department to get this process completed at the very
earliest.
LAKSHMIBAI NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF PHYSICAL EDUCATION (LNIPE)
29. LNIPE, Gwalior is an autonomous body under the control of the Department of Sports.
LNIPE, is the national apex institution for Physical Education (PE) teachers training, National
Physical Fitness Plan and PE in school curriculum. The objectives of LNIPE are as follows:–
➢ To prepare highly qualified leaders in the field of Physical Education,
➢ Sports/Games and other inter-disciplinary subjects.
➢ To serve as a centre of excellence and innovation in Physical Education, and to
undertake, promote and disseminate research and also publish literature in this field.
➢ To provide professional and academic leadership to other institutions in the field of
Physical Education
➢ To provide vocational guidance and placement service to the people in this field.
➢ To promote mass participation in Physical Education activities.
30. Presently, LNIPE has 863 students. The Committee came to know that the Plan allocation
amounting to `40 crores stagnated during the BE 2014-15 and also at RE 2014-15. However, it has
increased to `45 crores in BE 2015-16. The Committee has noted that a normal increase in BE
2015-16 is to meet establishment expenditure. The Committee notes that the budget allocations
have been sufficiently utilized but feels that the allocations will not be enough for meeting
the projected activities and requirement of the Institute such as laying of squash court,

9
tennis court, gymnasium, swimming pool, astro turf, boys hostels, girls hostels, etc. The
Committee, therefore, recommends for the enhanced budget allocation to accomplish the
proposed activities/works within the stipulated time frame.
SPECIAL CASH AWARDS
31. Special cash awards are being provided to winners in International Sporting events and their
coaches to encourage and motivate outstanding sportspersons for higher achievements and to
attract the younger generation to take sports as a career. Cash Awards are given to coaches who
have trained the medal winners for at least 240 days immediately preceding the tournament. Award
money to a coach is 50% of the award money given to the sportsperson coached. In case, there
is more than one coach the award money is distributed among them equally.

CONCLUSION
66. The execution of a mega sporting event helps in developing infrastructure, generating
employment, securing inflow of foreign capital and thus contributes significantly to the economic
development of a country. Therefore, if can be said that the impact of sports on the society is
multi-dimensional.
65. Despite varied and concerted efforts, the performance of Indian sports at the International
level is not very convincing. Therefore, a few steps may be recommended to make these initiatives
more comprehensive, like
➢ The allocation of funds, as the percentage of budget, should be increased rationally to
broad-base sports in the country.
➢ Sports should be made as an integral part of the education system to inculcate sports
culture from the school level.
➢ The effectiveness of the developmental projects should be evaluated periodically.
➢ Uniformity should be maintained in sports specific activities of various States of India
to provide equal participation opportunity to its citizens.
➢ A structure of good management, control and exercise should be incorporated to make
the system transparent and accountable.
66. The Committee feels that to revive sports culture, the Government should revisit the
sporting framework of India. This is also the need of the hour as India is reaping benefits
of demographic dividend in the form of young population which can easily be channelized
to sports and games for achieving better results. Otherwise, achievement of goals by
utilizing the available immense potential of the country in sports would be difficult to
realize. For achieving improved performance in sports internationally the government needs
to play a proactive role in promoting sports in India to establish the country as a sporting
nation. The Committee hopes that with improved sporting infrastructure and infusion of
latest technology in training of sportpersons India would show better results at the next
Olympics to be held at Rio in Brazil.

The Committee notes with concern that there has been a gap between the projected
demands and the actual allocated funds during all these years. The Committee, therefore,
keeping in view the major emphasis of the Department during 2015-16 for preparation of
sports persons and teams for Rio Olympics 2016 feels that the Department should
endeavour to get enhancement of the fund at the RE stage so that the gap in allocation is

of our preparation as well as performance at the next Olympics and initiatives to be taken
by the Department also to tap non-governmental sources. (Para 11)

agency between the Centre and the States, and also acted as monitoring agency, it is not

The Committee notes that although of late there has been slight improvement in the
performance of India’s sportspersons at international events but it is incomparable with the

that could not be utilized fully. It was perhaps on account of such a poor pattern that the
allocation for BE 2015-16 has also been reduced to `25 crores. The Committee, accordingly
recommends that Department should take initiatives to expedite the submission of
utilization certificates by the implementing agencies in time so that the allocation pattern
is not affected adversely in future. (Para 35)
RAJIV GANDHI KHEL ABHIYAN (RGKA)
The Committee appreciates the launching of RGKA a centrally sponsored scheme in
place of earlier PYKKA scheme for its novel objectives of expanding and developing sports
specifically in the rural areas. This is a major Scheme to provide sports complexes for both
outdoor and I indoor disciplines in all the 6545 blocks 634 districts in phased manner over
a period of five years. Out in view of such humongous objectives of the scheme, the
performance both physical and financial during the last year does not inspire any confidence
that we will be able to achieve the objectives within the five years. The problem of pending
UCs should not be taken as an excuse in implementing such a flagship scheme.
(Para 41)
This Scheme has to work in convergence with different other schemes implemented by
different Ministries, the Committee feels that there may be possibility of lack of adequate co-
ordination and synergy in pooling the resources and the efforts for implementing this Scheme
effectively. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that a coordination mechanism especially
for this scheme should be put in place to obviate any such possibility. (Para 42)
Thirdly, the Committee is intrigued to note that `200 crore in the Plan allocation for
RGKA during BE 2014-15 was reduced to `85 crores in RE and even the reduced allocation
could not be utilized fully. The reason being given non-receipt of Utilization Certificates by
the implementing agencies. The Committee finds this disheartening. Interestingly, in BE
2015-16, the Plan allocation for this scheme which was `200 crore in BE 2014-15 has been
reduced to `95 crores. The Committee fails to understand with this meager allocation how
the objectives of the Department are going to achieved in time. We have more than 50%
reduced allocation for this Scheme and we are not able to spend even the highly reduced
allocation that too on technical procedural grounds as UCs. The Committee finds that if this
is the state of affairs in respect of this Scheme then future of this scheme remains highly
bleak. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to make all out efforts to
implement this scheme with the required zeal and dedication. (Para 43)
SPORTS UNIVERSITY IN NORTH-EAST
It has come to the notice of the Committee that till date no expenditure has been
incurred on account of National Sports University. The Committee recommends that setting
up of the proposed National Sports University is accomplished within the stipulated time and
the Department will go all out in this endeavour and make it a novel scheme. (Para 45)

20
NATIONAL SPORTS TALENT SERARCH SCHEME (NSTSS)
The Committee recommends that the requisite initiatives should be taken by the
Department to accomplish NSTSS within the stipulated time frame and all hurdles coming
in the way of the execution of the scheme are taken care of effectively so as to make it
a note-worthy scheme. (Para 47)
ENHANCEMENT IN SPORTS FACILITY OF JAMMU AND KASHMIR
The Committee appreciates the allocations of funds for expanding and development
of sports in Jammu and Kashmir which has been ridden with terror and insurgency for
quite a long time. The Committee hopes that improved sports culture in the region would
provide better channels to the youth to show their talent. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department will work to get the proposed scheme implemented within
the required time and all impediments are overcome adequately, making this a worth-while
scheme. (Para 49)
PROMOTION OF SPOR TS AMONG DISABLED
The Committee gathered that a three days 15 th National Para-Athletics Meet was held
at Ghaziabad (U.P.) in March, 2015. The Committee is surprised that the complete apathy
and negligence was shown towards the para-athletes during this 15 th National Para-Athletics
Championship. The last Para-Olympic national Championship was held in 2013 at Bengaluru.
A win at this event of Ghaziabad would have ensured that athletes qualify to participate in
upcoming Para-games to be held in May in Delhi and then make a bid to Para-Olympic
Games in 2016. The Committee strongly recommends that a thorough inquiry may be made
to identify the persons responsible for this kind of fiasco and for taking appropriate action
against the persons concerned and to ensure that this does not recur in future. The
Committee desires to have a status note on it at the earliest. (Para 52)
The Committee has also gathered that the Paralympics Committee of India (PCI),
owing to lackadaisical attitude and apathy towards its athletes, has been suspended by the
International Paralympics Committee (IPC). The Committee also shows its concern for
chaotic condition prevailing in PCI for several years mostly due to individual conflicts and
proper management, etc. (Para 53)
PENSION TO MERITORIOUS SPORTS PERSONS
The Committee fails to get any reason for this reduction in RE from the
Department. The Committee doubts whether this scheme of the Department will achieve the
desired result in the current fiscal. The Committee, therefore, feels that a review may be
made of the scheme to include necessary ingredients in it to make it more comprehensive.
(Para 54)
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT IN SPORTS
The Committee is surprised to find that `10 crore was allocated in BE 2014-15 and
it got reduced to `0.35 crore in RE stage of year 2014-15 owing to receipt of less number
of viable names. The Committee hopes that this scheme of the Department will achieve the
desired result in the current fiscal for what it has been meant for. (Para 55)

21
NATIONAL SPORTS DEVELOPMENT FUND (NSDF)
The Committee finds it disheartening that the budgetary allocation was reduced to
`3.75 crores at RE stage of year 2014-15 due to non-receipt of U.Cs by implementing
agencies and reiterates its earlier observations that U.Cs may be liquidated at the earliest
for the better utilization of funds. (Para 56)
NATIONAL DOPE TESTING LABORATORY
The Committee notes with satisfaction for the projected outcomes of achieving drug
free sports environment to the extent possible. (Para 57)
NATIONAL ANTI DOPING AGENCY (NADA)
The Committee appreciates that functioning of NADA and hopes that our
sportspersons get complete information on the guidance regarding banned drugs in sports
so that they are not misled in this regard. The Committee also hopes that this scheme of
the Department will achieve the desired result in the current fiscal only if it gets full
support as the by way of providing sufficient funds and required expertise. (Para 58)
WORLD DOPING AGENCY (WDA)
The Committee hopes that this scheme of the Department will achieve the desired
result in the current fiscal for what it has been meant for. (Para 59)
SAI STADIA RENOV ATION
Such a meagre allocation for renovation, major and minor, of the SAI Stadia does not
inspire confidence that it will be sufficient for our huge stadia spread all over. The
Committee hopes that this scheme of the Department will achieve the desired result in the
current fiscal for what it has been meant for. (Para 60)
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF SPORTS SCIENCE AND SPORTS MEDICINE
The Committee hopes that this scheme of the Department will become functional
during the current fiscal. (Para 61)
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF COACHING EDUCATION
The Committee is surprised to see that such a significant scheme which is highly
needed in the country could not be finalized for the last two years. It is not clear why the
provisions are being made for this scheme in the Budget when scheme is under finalization;
why not make allocation in the year when the scheme has been finalized. Blocking funds
in such a way and then surrendering, is not a healthy fiscal practice at all. The Committee
does not understand why this scheme could not be finalized. The Committee recommends
that finalization of this scheme should be expedited. (Para 62)
NATIONAL PHYSICAL FITNESS PROGRAMME-RESOURCE CENTRE AT LNIPE GWALIOR
The Committee hopes that this scheme of the Department will become functional
during the current fiscal. (Para 63)

22
SCHEME FOR IDENTIFICATION AND NURTURING OF SPORTS TALENT
The Committee hopes that this scheme of the Department will become functional
during the current fiscal. (Para 64)
NATIONAL WELFARE FUNDS FOR SPORTS PERSONS
The Committee feels that this Scheme is a novel scheme but the allocation of
`1 crore appears to be ridiculous in view of the large number of eminent sportspersons,
having brought laurels to the country, are languishing in penury selling tea, vegetables, etc.
in the street. This is highly unbecoming to their status as well as to the country’s prestige.
This also demotivates our budding sportspersons and their parents to allow their children
to take up sports. Therefore, the Committee is of the considered opinion that all possible
help should be extended to our eminent former sportspersons in all possible manner and the
allocation should be increased at least ten times to begin with. (Para 65)
CONCLUSION
The Committee feels that to revive sports culture, the government should revisit the
sporting framework of India. This is also the need of the hour as India is reaping benefits
of demographic dividend in the form of young population which can easily be channelized
to sports and games for achieving better results. Otherwise, achievement of goals by
utilizing the available immense potential of the country in sports would be difficult to
realize. For achieving improved performance in sports internationally the government needs
to play a proactive role in promoting sports in India to establish the country as a sporting
nation. The Committee hopes that with improved sporting infrastructure and infusion of
latest technology in training of sportspersons India would show better results at the next
Olympics to be held at Rio in Brazil. (Para 68)

INTRODUCTION

I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human
Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the report on
its behalf, present this Twenty Seventh Report on Action Taken by the Government on the
recommendations contained in its 7th Report on “Demands for Grants” (1994-95) of
Ministry of Human Resource Development (Department of Women and Child Develop-
ment).

on Human Resource Development was presented to Rajya Sabha on 22nd April, 1994 and
laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 22nd April, 1994. Replies of Government on all the
recommendations contained in the report, received from the Deptt. of Women and Child
Development were considered by the Committee and this report was adopted at its sitting
held on 31st May, 1995.

CHAPTER-I
REPORT

The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the
recommendations contained in its Seventh Report on Demands for Grants of the Ministry of
Human Resource Development (Department of Women and Child Development) for the
year 1994-95 which was presented to Rajya Sabha on 22.4.94 and laid on the Table of Lok
Sabha on 22.4.94.

2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of all the
recommendations contained in the Report. They have been categorised as follows:

(i) Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: para

(ii) Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the Government's replies: para 1. 2 4. 6, 9, 10, 14, 15, 17, 19, 21, 22, 27, 30, 32,
36, 37, 38, 42.

(iii) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government
have not been accepted by the Committee: 11, 12, 16, 20, 28, 29, 33, 34, 35, 39, 43, 44.

(iv) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government
are still awaited: Nil.

3. The Committee will now deal with the Action Taken by the Government on some of
its recommendations.

Working Women’s Hostele
Recommendation (Para No. 11)

The Committee is of the view that the though there is acute shortage of working
women’s hostel in the country the Department could not achieve the physical targets. During
1993-94, but ambitious targets have been fixed for 1994-95. The Committee desires that
effective steps should be taken by the Department to achieve the targets set for 1994-95.

Ministry’s reply :

The reason for non-fulfilment of physical target in number of hostels in 1993-94 was the
steep rise in construction costs. However, capacity achievement over 82% and under-
utilisation was more than the BE/RE. To achieve the target of sanctioning of 60 additional
hostels to provide accommodation to 3000 working women during 1994-95 all the State
Governments and Union Territories have already been advised to send the proposals of all
suitable organisations. 50 proposals have already been received and are being processed.
Comments of the Committee

The Committee is not satisfied with the reply given by the Department and hence
reiterating its recommendation suggests that all-out efforts be made to achieve the physical
target.
Recommendation (Para No. 12) ~

In view of the frequent complaints received about mismanagement of the hostels
receiving grants and assistance from the Government, the Committee felt that there was
need for evolving some system of monitoring so as to control any sort of irregularities in
these hostels. For-this purpose, the Committee recommended that a Government representa-
tive be included on the Board of Management of each of such hostels.

1


Ministry’s reply

“Since inception of the Scheme in 1972-73, 685 hostels for 44,960 working women have
already been sanctioned upto 31.3.1994. It will, thus, not be practicable to nominate a
Member of the Central Government on the Hostel Management Committee of each and
every Hostel. It has already been provided in the scheme that the Hostel Management
Committee shall have a, representative of the State Government/UT Administration and the
Central Social Welfare Board and /or State Social Welfare Advisory Board. The Scheme
also provides for representation of the residents of the hostel. The Hostel Management
Committee is required to meet at least once in three months. The present system seems to
be adequate to handle the situation.”

Comments of the Committee

The Committee expresses it isfaction over the present system of monitoring as it
has utterly failed to contain gross mismanagement, irregularities and, victi tion of inmates
rempant in the working women’s hostels. It, therefore, is of the view that an effective
alternative mechanism is required to be evolved by the Government to monitor the

functioning of various hostels.

Atrocities against Women
Recommendation (Para No. 16)

The Committee expresses its concern over the increasing number of cases of atrocities
against women and recommends that Government should conduct some review of these
publicity programmes to find out whether these are sufficient to create a significant impact
on the public mind.

Ministry’s reply

“Owing to the diverse nature of the programmes funded so far, this Deptt. has not so
far carried out any review of the nature suggested by the Committee. However, now since
most of the assistance under the programme is being given for legal literacy programmes,
this Deptt. would consider reviewing these legal literacy programmes in the future.”

Comments of the Committee .

Ever-increasing incidence of atrocities against women, specially in the urban areas, is
not only a matter of serious concern, but also a clear-cut reflection of the fact that the
programme has miserably failed to deliver the goods. Inspite of this, the Department does
not seem to have shown any concern as is obvious in its comments. The Committee is not
happy about this kind of apathetic attitude of the Deptt. and suggests that a periodic
evaluation of the efficacy of all the programmes in general, and this programme is particular,
must be undertaken to achieve the desired result.

Indira Mahila Yojana

Recommendation (Para No. 20)

The Committee expresses its deep concern over the fact that though the scheme was
announced in the President’s Address in 1991, till this date it has not been operationalised.
Ministry’s reply

“The Department has made concerted efforts to get the necessary approval for
launching the Yojana. At present, the EFC Memo on Indira Mahila Yojana (IMY) for 200
blocks in the country is pending with the Planning Commission for its approval.


Comments of the Committee

The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the tardy progress of this scheme
which, although conceived way back in 1991, is yet to take off. The Committee, therefore,
trusts that Government would make all necessary efforts to seek its clearance from the
Planning Commission and launch it at the earliest.

Mahila Samridhi Yojana
Recommendation (Para No. 24)
The Committee is of the view that various programmes under the Mahila Samridhi
Yojana are implemented keeping in view the welfare of rural women, whereas, poor women
in urban areas, who are also in need of assistance, are not covered under it. The Committee

recommends that requirements of needy urban women belonging to the weaker sections
should also be kept in mind while framing and implementing schemes for women’s welfare.

Ministry’s reply
“Noted. The Government will review the scheme during the year 1994 and examine
various suggestions being given to strengthen the scheme further.”

Comments of the Committee

The Committee desires that the Department should complete the requisite formulities at
the earlies in this regard.

Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)
Recommendation (Para Nos. 28 & 29)

The main thrust of ICDS programme is on the provision of Anganwadis in every village
and urban slum areas. Generally, there is one Anganwadi for a population of 1000 in rural
areas and urban slum areas and of about 700 in tribal areas, which is run by an Anganwadi
worker, a female voluntary worker and a helper. By the end of 1993, 3120 ICDS projects
were sanctioned which benefited about 1.94 crores children and women. For the year 1994-
95 an outlay of Rs. 426.00 crores has been approved for the ICDS and 200 new projects are
likely to start. The Committee feels that a big portion of the increased outlay is likely to be
absorbed in the increased honorarium to Anganwadi workers. Therefore, the Committee
feels that the amount available for the projected expansion of the scheme to cover new areas
is likely to be insufficient. Of 5239 blocks, 2119 blocks remain to be covered. At the rate, of
200 projects per year, it will take another 10 years for all blocks to be covered. To expedite
the process, any shortfall in the projected expansion by the end of the 8th Plan should be
properly estimated and additional allocations made.

The relative success of the ICDS scheme in improving child health and lowering IMR is
due to its decentralized and popular structure. Probably because of this, ICDS is being
increasingly seen as an umbrella organisation within which other schemes could be
incorporated. Thus early childhood education is now a part of ICDS. There is a new scheme
for adolescent girls; and creches and day care centres are sought to be made a part of ICDS.
Indira Mahila Yojana, in its revised form, will become a component of it. Separate
allocations have been proposed for these schemes by the Department. But the National
Creche Fund has only been notified. Allocation of Rs. 8 crores for Indira Mahila Yojana has
not yet been approved. Therefore, the Committee recommends that until and unless
separate additional allocations have been obtained for these additional components, ICDS
should concentrate on strengthening and expansion its own. structure with whatever
allocations it may get. The proposal to entrust a percentage of ICDS schemes to NGOs
should be properly assessed before it is implemented, since, in the absence of community-
based monitoring arrangements, it would be difficult to ensure accountability of NGOs.


Ministry’s reply

It is proposed to sanction 200 projects during the year 1994-95. In order to sanction 200
projects and to maintain the existing projects, the Plan outlay of Rs. 426 crores has been
approved for the ICDS which is adequate to meet the requirements. However, for
universalisation of ICDS during the 8th Plan period, we would require an additional amount
of Rs. 1166.27 crores in the Central plan and an additional amount of Rs. 1379.96 crores in
the State outlays on nutrition during the Plan period.

As mentioned against Para 28, the outlay provided for 1994-95 would be adequate to
meet the requirement of additional 200 blocks of ICDS project and to maintain the existing
ICDS projects. A number of effective steps including sanction of additional AWCs,
construction of godowns/anganwadi buildings, provision of storage containers have been
taken by the Department for strengthening ICDS scheme directly involvement of NGOs in
directly implementing ICDS projects has been considered vital to strengthening community
participation under the scheme. To ensure that only competent NGOs are entrusted with
such projects. State Governments have been given the discretion to identify competent
NGOs with proven track record.

Comments of the Committee

In view of the prospects of the universalisation of ICDS, the Committee feels that the
financial allocation earmarked for it is not adequate. Therefore, it suggests that allocations
for this scheme should be adequately enhanced. The Committee expresses its concern over
integration of more and more components under umbrella of ICDS without providing
adequate resources for each of them. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that due
consideration should be given to this aspect.

Recommendation (Para Nos. 33 & 34)

The Committee observes that out of the three components of ICDS, namely executive,
workers and recipients, two do not appear to be happy with the service. Therefore,
monitoring system should be strengthened to ensure proper functioning of the ICDS to the
satisfaction of all its components.

The Committee feels that since it is a Central project, public representatives should also
be involved for proper monitoring of the scheme.

Ministry’s reply

The Department has adopted an improve management information system to monitor
the implementation of the ICDS scheme. The Monthly Progress Reports on each aspect of
the Scheme is received by the Department straight from the projects which are analysed with
respect to crucial indicators on a quarterly and half yearly basis. Monitoring system has been
strengthened to reflect the frequency as the delivery of services and gender specific
information of the beneficiaries. In addition to these reports on performance of projects, the
Department is also receiving Quarterly Monitoring Reports on health aspects of the scheme
from the Central Technical Committee. These Quarterly Monitoring Reports are generated
by Central Technical Committee on the basis of Monthly Monitoring Reports received from
Primary Health Centres and analysis is carried out for variable such as provision of
supplementary nutrition, pre-school education, health check-up and referral services, child
and mother mortality, existing status of malnutrition of children, staff position, their recruitment
and vacancy position and immunisation coverage. The State exhibiting poor performance in
respect of any of these indicators are promptly addressed to rectify the suitably by intensifying
efforts and close monitoring. In addition to the existing monitoring system at the Central and
State level, the community based monitoring mechanism has been recently evolved. The States
have been asked to constitute Bal Vikas Mahila Samities at the village, block and district levels
for involvement of elected women representatives of Panchayats in monitoring all the child and
women programme being implemented in their area of jurisdiction.


Comments of the Committee

The Committee notes that the Department has not responded on the ICDS workers
being not happy with the services they are being over burdened with the integration/addition
of new schemes to the ICDS for which they are not being adequately compensated, suggests
that efforts should be made to remove the grievances of the ICDS workers.

Creches/Day Care Centres
Recommendation (Para No. 35)

This scheme was started in 1975 to provide day care services to children in the age
group of 0—5 years of those families whose monthly income does not exceed Rs. 1800 per
month. The scheme is implemented through the Central Social Welfare Board, the Indian
Council for Child Welfare and Bharatiya Adim Jati Sewak Sangh. During the year 1993-94,
a total amount of Rs. 23.05 crores was sanctioned to benefit about 3 lakh children. The
same amount has been allotted in the budgetary provisions for this year. The Committee
reaffirms its earlier observations made in its third report about the Bharatiya Adim Jati
Sewak Sangh regarding the need for conducting an enquiry into the affairs of the Sangh.

Ministry's reply
“During the current financial year a budget provision of Rs. 23.05 crores has been made

under the scheme of Creches and Day Care Centres. An evaluation of the creches
programme by competent professionals is underway.”

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is constrained to observe that the Department has taken the
recommendation in a very casual and cavalier manner by eschewing unequivocal reply on
conducting an enquiry into the affairs of the Bharatiya Adim Jati Sewak Sangh. Many more
cases of malpractices and irregularities in creche programmes being run by Indian Council
for Child Welfare, Central Social Welfare Board, apart from Bharatiya Adim Jati Sewak
Sangh, coming to the fore, has added to the urgency and necessity of such an enquiry.
Although the Committee has been subsequently informed that the inquiry has been initiated,
it underlines the need to expedite the process.

Recommendation (Para No. 39)

It has been observed that since Creche and Day Care Centres are non-expanding
schemes, the budgetary allocation remains stagnant. With escalation of costs, this may cause
maintenance grants to existing centres to dry up. Therefore, even non-plan allocation should
be enhanced. Also, until the National Creche Fund actually starts functioning, some scope
for expansion should be kept in the budgetary allocations under this head, in view of the
urgent need for such centres.

Ministry’s reply

The Department will sanction new creches under National Creche Fund. The National
Creche Fund has been set up. In accordance with Government policy, non-plan expenditure
is to be curtailed as far as possible. The Committee, however, would be happy to know that
the norms of nutrition as well as honorarium of the creche, scheme have been revised
upwards and adequate. provision for this expenditure has been made on the plan side with
the approval of the Planning Commission.


Comments of the Committee

The Committee is happy to note that the National Cultural Fund would start functioning
from this year, however, there may be many areas where NGOs may not be available for
running creches. In such areas where there are creches/day care centres under the old
system, these centres should not be allowed to suffer.

SAARC Decade of Girl Child

Recommendation (Para No. 41)

The Committee notes with concern that the SAARC Decade of the Girl Child, except
for one scheme introduced as a component of ICDS for the adolescent girl, has not found
any reflection in the budget. Schemes to improve the nutritional status of the girl-child and
schemes to prevent their dropping out from schools may be formulated. As for the National
Plan of Action for children, the Committee was informed by the Secretary that there was no
separate allocation for this in the Department’s budget because this plan is to be
implemented by different ministries and departments and Women and Child Development
Department is only the coordinator. Since, however, there is little evidence of such
coordinating activities so far, the Committee is constrained to conclude that this has not
made much headway so far and recommends its speeder planning and implementation.

Ministry’s reply

Government takes note of the concerns expressed by the Standing Committee at the
mere token provision for the National Plan of Action of Girl Child in the budgets of this
Department. We would like to clarify that the implementation of the Plan of Action and the
attainment of goals that have been quantified in the Plan of Action constitute the joint
responsibility of all Ministries/Departments of the Government and the modal Department
of Women and Child Development implementing programmes having a bearing on the girl
child. A token provision has been kept in mind the future need, if any, of introducing
special interventions for filling up critical gaps as and when felt necessary. This plan and the
National Plan of Action for Children would help the Department of Women and Child
Development to coordinate and orchestrate the working of various programmes run different
Ministries/Departments for the purpose of reaching the goals of children and girl children.

The Standing Committee has referred to the need for schemes to improve the
nutritional status of the girl child and-preventing school dropouts. It is submitted that girl
children upto the age of 6 years are already included within the ICDS programme which is
the world’s largest integrated child development programme and the specific problem of
school dropouts amongst girls is addressed through the Adolescent Girl Programme which
covers school dropout adolescent girls in the age group 11—18 years. This Department is
coordinating a special gender disaggregated monitoring of the ICDS Programme, the
programmes of the Department of Education, the programmes of the Department of Health
and Family Welfare and those of the other departments. Government, through the
Department of Education, extends special incentives to the girl children viz. free supply of
text-books, special hostel facilities, scholarships, uniforms, appointment of lady teachers etc.
for coordinating the entire effort, there is an inter-ministerial Coordination Committee under
the Secretary (WCD) at the Central level. We have also advised the State Government to
draw up similar action plans and set up similar State level Coordination Committees.

The Committee observes that the Department in its reply has not given any details of
the schemes/programmes initiated by it. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommen-
dation.

Food & Nutrition Board
Recommendation (Para No. 43)

The Committee observes that the thrust of the policy should be on raising the
nutritional status of the population through ICDS, as well as nutritional education. In this
contest, the Committee recommends revival of the scheme of supply of milk to the under-
nourished school children.

Ministry's reply

The thrust of the policy of Food & Nutrition Board is already on raising nutritional
status of the population through nutritional education. For this purpose, demonstration
programmes are arranged by the field units of FNB and also training is given to housewives
and adolescent girls in nutrition education and preservation of fruits and vegetables.
Integrated Nutrition Education Camps and Orientation Training Courses are organised by
the field units of FNB for the supervisory and grassroot functionaries of different
Departments of State Government concerned with health and nutrition education. The
recommendation regarding supply of milk to school children has been sent to Department of
Educaiton for necessary action.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee finds that the Department in its reply has stated that the recommenda-
tion regarding supply of milk to school children has been sent to the Department of
Education for necessary action. The Committee feels that the Department should see to it
that the scheme of the supply of milk is revived and for this it should pursue the matter with
the Department of Education effectively.

Proliferation of Schemes

Recommendation (Para No. 44)

The Committee feels that, year after year, the focus of attention of the Deptt. keeps on
changing from one scheme to another and there seems to be no long-term perspective.
Therefore, the Committee recommends that instead of framing new schemes every year and
letting the earlier ones to just continue, the Deptt. should concentrate on some major
schemes and work to achieve the targets through suitable action plan.

Ministry’s reply

“Over the years, the Department has formulated policies and programmes dealing with
various aspects of the development of women and children according to changing needs,
imperatives and perspectives. The Department, thus, has a long-term perspective in both the
sectors. In the fields of child development, the Department plays a nodal role in
coordinating the development of children in various sectors, besides implementing its own
programme of Nutrition, Integrated Child Development and Early Childhood Education.
The Department’s continuing focus has been on working as the national machinery for
women, promoting the incorporation of women, as well as for moulding societal attitudes.
Besides this, the Department has a three-pronged approach to Women’s Development
through its own programmes targeted at training and economic empowerment, provision of


8

support services and awareness generation. Thus, the approach is a mix of advocacy and
action. However, as and when the need arises, new activities are taken up by the
Department. For example, the political empowerment of women as a result of 73rd
Constitution Amendment, has opened up possibilities of fundamental and significant
initiatives to be taken jn this field. Similarly, the adoption of National Nutrition Policy in
1993 has resul.ed in 8. greater focus on the issues of nutrition surveillance and preparation of
a Plan of Action cutting across different sections.”

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is of the view that the Department should devise long term plan
perspectives and concentrate on continuing with them considerably for a longer time so that
their benefits could percolate down to the targeted populace. Conceiving new and new
programmes, year after year, without giving them a practical shape is not a healthy
phenomenon and yields nothing. The reply of the Deptt. does not indicate any specific
action proposed to be taken on its recommendations. The Committee, therefore, reiterates
that the focus of the Department should be on strengthening the on-going schemes and it
should not keep on shifting its priorities.
