X.  TECHNICAL EDUCATION-QUALITY IMPROVEMENT PROGRAMME (TEQIP) 
10.1 The Department submitted that AICTE is conscious of the shortage as well as the 
availability of quality faculty in technical institutions. Apart from prescribing norms and standard 
for faculty requirement and cadre ratio for giving approval to technical institutions, AICTE is 
making concerted efforts to upgrade the skills of faculty by way of providing opportunities to 
faculty through short term and long term quality improvement program conducted in QIP Centers 
promoted by it in various parts of the country.   
10.2 The Department further added that under its Quality Improvement Scheme (AQIS), AICTE 
has taken several initiatives to promote quality in Technical Education through Research, 
Institutional and Faculty Development Program (RIFD) with ultimate aim to attract and motivate 
young generation to join faculty, pursue higher study and carry out research. The facult y is given 
enormous chances to improve their educational qualification under Quality Improvement Program 
(QIP), and develop research under Research Promotion Scheme (RPS). Faculty Development 
Program (FDP) also provides opportunities to faculty member of AICTE approved 
Colleges/Institutions to facilitate up-gradation of knowledge and skill. In addition, under Travel 
Grant Program (TG) meritorious faculty gets opportunities to interact at International Level 
Seminars, and Symposia, both within and outside India, Teachers from AICTE approved 
Technical Institutions/University departments are eligible for this grant. Various Schemes also 
provides financial assistance to faculty members for quality education/ research and capac ity 
building programs as follows: 
i. Quality Improvement Program (QIP) : To upgrade the expertise and capabilities of the 
faculty members of the degree level institutions in the country. The aim is to enable the 
teachers to acquire Master’s/Doctoral degrees. Scholar -ships are paid @ Rs.9000/- per month 
for M.Tech (Polytechnic) and Rs.15,000/- per month for Ph.D. for a maximum period of two 
and three years respectively. 
ii. Research Promotion Scheme (RPS) : Is aimed to create research ambience in the Institutes 
by promoting research in engineering sciences and innovations in established and newer 
technologies; and to encourage  Master’s and Doctoral candidates to augment the quality of 
faculty and research personnel in the country. Maximum grant per research scheme is 
Rs.25,00,000/- for a duration of three years. 
iii. Adjunct Faculty:  To appoint Adjunct Faculty for bringing external perspective to regular 
teaching to make classes more interesting and to enrich knowledge of regular faculty 
members too. The limit of funding is Rs. 6 Lakhs/ Faculty/ Institute. 
iv. Trainee Teacher Scheme : The scheme is intended towards attracting bright Undergraduate 
and Postgraduate students to teaching profession by providing scholarships for M.Tech/Ph.D 

Fellowships and assured job for advancing their professional growth. The maximum funding 
is Rs.2.5 lakhs over and above other financial assistance/scholarship, if any.  The duration of 
the project is for three years. Trainee Teacher Scheme was launched in 2016.  
v. Faculty Development Program:  The Faculty Development Program intends to provide 
financial assistance to facilitate up-gradation of knowledge and skill. Total funding of Rs.7 
lakhs is provided and the project duration is 2 weeks. 
vi. Scheme Of Seminar Grant (SG):  Scheme provides financial assistance to institutions for 
organizing seminar/ workshop at National and International level in various fields of 
Technical education and also extending opportunities to the academicians and working 
professionals for sharing the knowledge, experience, innovation and inventions. Total funding 
is up to Rs. 2 lakhs for National and Rs.3 lakhs for International seminars. 
vii. Scheme of Travel Grant (TG): The scheme is aimed at promoting research and development

visiting faculty as well as using online mode of teaching to overcome these shortages. To make the

11.11 The Committee expresses its concern over the shortage of faculty positions in all the 
institutions including the private ones.  It points out that there can be only two possibilitie s, 
either our young talented students are not attracted towards the teaching profession or the 
recruitment process is a prolonged one and involves too many procedural formalities. In 
either case, the Department being the nodal authority for the entire country so far as higher 
education sector is concerned has to take proactive role so as to expedite the filling up  a 
existing vacancies.  
11.12 The Committee has been voicing its concern from time to time on the acute shortag e 
of faculty in higher educational institutions across the country. The Committee is anguishe d 
to find out that all kinds of institutions right from well established Central Universities to 
those set up recently, State universities as well as private universities, premier institutions 
like IITs, NITs and IIMs, this problem has emerged as the biggest handicap for the 
development and growth of Higher Education vis-a-vis maintaining the quality of education. 
Situation continues to be grim with no improvement being foreseen in the near future. The 

Committee points out that the availability of adequate and qualified faculty is a pre-requ isite 
for quality education. So far, the efforts of the Department, the regulatory bodies like  UGC, 
AICTC etc. and the universities and other institutions have not been adequate enough  to 
reach a satisfaction level. The Committee therefore impress upon all the stakeholders to 
expedite and ensure that shortages are eliminated or minimized. 
 11.13 The Committee, however, recognizes the steps taken by Department like increase in 
the retirement age up to 65 years and improvement of salary structures.  
11.14 The Committee recommends that recruitment process should start well in ad vance 
before the post is vacated so that after retirement, the newly recruited person takes up  
position immediately. The Ministry should work in tandem with Institutions to have this 
exercise on yearly basis and recruitment must be done in advance so that shor tage does not 
develop into crisis. While taking note of the steps taken up by the Department for filling u p 
the vacancies, the Committee observes  that  in order to make the teaching profession m ore 
attractive, the government's effort to allow and encourage the faculty to undertake 
consultancy and the financial support, for setting up start up have to be lucrative enough so 
as to meet the expectations of the aspirants. The Committee accordingly directs the 
Department of Higher Education to explore the possibilities and take necessary steps on 
priority basis. 
11.15 The Committee further recommends that in order to improve the position there 
should be an increase in the number of research fellowships for M.Phil , PhD and Post 
Doctoral Program to create potential faculty for universities and colleges and also incre ase 
the number of fellowship and amount through NET.  The Department should also provide 
an opportunity to the teachers to present papers in academic conferences seminars or 
participate in workshops; exchange knowledge and ideas; and the young faculty member  to 
spend a short period of two weeks to two months at institutions of their choice for a better 
academic exposure.

12.7 The Scheme has the following broad contours:

XV.   MISCELLANEOUS 
National Testing Service 
15.1 A new initiative to create a specialized independent, professional and specialist 
organization named National Testing Service for conducting all entrance examinations and 
fellowship tests for admission into higher educational institutions or for grant of fellowships and 
such other benefits is being considered in consultation with all stakeholders. The objectives of the 
NTS are-  
a. To conduct efficient, transparent and international standards tests in order to access the 
competency of candidates for admission, and recruitment purposes.  
b. To undertake research on educational, professional and testing systems to identify gaps in the 
knowledge systems and take steps for bridging them.  

c. To identify experts and institutions in setting examination questions.  
d. To produce and disseminate information and research on education and professional 
development standards 
 
15.2 In order to start its operation, the NTS would be provided a onetime grant of Rs. 50.00 
crore (Recurring- Rs.10 crore and Non-recurring - Rs. 40 crore ) in 2017-18.  From 2018-19 
onwards, NTS would be funded by the exams fees of over 40 lakh students.  Considering the exam 
fee paid by students in the entrance examinations currently being held, and the fees concession or 
exemption for SC/ STs /PWDs and girl candidates provided, average fees per student is estimated 
to be Rs. 500.  Since approximately 40 lakh students would appear in the exams conducted by 
NTS each year, Rs 200 crore would be generated by NTS each year, which will be sufficient to 
meet its recurring and non- recurring expenditure. A CEE (Committee on Establishment 
Expenditure) Memorandum has been prepared and sent to the all concerned Ministry/Department 
for comments.  
15.3 The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Department to create new 
specialized organization for conducting entrance examinations and fellowships for admiss ion 
into higher educational institutions.  The Committee believes that this testing agency wou ld 
be able to meet its expenditure and conduct examinations in a free and fair mann er.  The  
Committee  also  hopes that  this  agency  would  make  the  examination  reliable .

15.6 In view of its observations in the foregoing paras the Committee further adds that 
quality assurance in higher education has to become top of policy agenda and education has 
to prepare graduates with new skills, broad knowledge base and a range of competenc ies to 
enter a more complex and interdependent world. Quality is a multi-dime nsional concept and 
several mechanisms for quality assurance and management at individual and institution al 
level are needed.  The Committee further points out that system of accountability and 
accreditation with a robust regulatory mechanism are essential to process of sustaining and 
improving quality and developing performance indicators and benchmarks for assessing 
outcomes in higher education.  The Committee accordingly, urges upon the Depar tment of 
Higher Education to take all measures so as to ensure the quality in higher educat ion 
matching will the global standards.

REPORT 
I INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Ministry of Women and Child Development came into existence as a separate Ministry 
w.e.f 30 th January, 2006.  It has the nodal responsibility to advance the rights and concerns of 
women and children who constitute 67.7 per cent of the country’s population as per 2011 census.  
The Ministry was constituted with the prime intention of addressing gaps in state action for women 
and children and for promoting inter-ministerial and inter-sectoral convergence to crea te gender 
equality and child-centred legislation, policies and programmes.  The function of the Ministr y is to 
promote the empowerment and protection of women and children and to ensure their equitable and 
wholesome development.  
1.2 The role of the Ministry includes policy formulation, programme implementation, 
coordination with other sectors, child and gender budgeting, data management, training and 
capacity building, reporting and monitoring on the status of women and children and their rights,   
The Ministry is the prime mover of inclusive programmes, policies, schemes and legislations for 
women and children and stands solely for securing the best interest of women and children.  
Promoting social and economic empowerment of women and ensuring survival, development, care 
and protection of children drive the Ministry’s agenda.  Principles of equity, justice and non -
discrimination guide the Ministry’s actions concerning women and children.  
1.3 The Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development, in her presentation before the 
Committee on 17 th February, 2017 gave an overview of the various programmes/schemes of the 
Ministry and achievements thereof.  She informed the Committee that the budget allocation for the 
year 2017-18 has been kept at Rs.22,094.67 crore, whereas the projected demand of the Ministry 
was for Rs.25,425.38 crore.  She pointed towards insufficiency of funds for the implementation of 
Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme on account of recommendations of the 
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) which has recommended discontinuation of the salary 
component (Rs.7,950 crore) of the regular ICDS field staff and has also disallowed construction of 
Aaganwadi Centres (AWCs) buildings (Rs. 4,662 crore) by the Ministry from ICDS funds causing 
a short fall of Rs.12612 crore under ICDS scheme.  According to the Secretary,  this would 
adversely affect the implementation of the scheme as the States/UTs may not be willing to take 
additional financial burden and that there would be infrastructural gaps in the construction  of 
Anganwadi Centre buildings and related facilities. The Secretary requested for 0.5 per cent 

budgetary support from Swachch Bharat Kosh for construction of toilet’s in AWCs without toilet 
facilities and for ensuring fund flow for infrastructure from convergent Ministries. 
1.4 Other important issues highlighted by the Secretary were the prevalence of underweight 
children in the 0-5 years age group, problem of anaemia, especially in the pregnant women and 
lactating mothers in the age group of 15-49 years and the declining child sex ratio (CSR) in the 
certain parts of the country.  According to the Secretary, serious attempts were required to be made 
to deal with these important issues.  The Committee was also informed of the initiatives relating to 
child protection services such as emergency outreach service-child line, railway child line, web 
portal for missing and found children, strengthening implementation of Beti Bachao Beti Padhao 
(BBBP) in the low CSR districts, expansion in operationalization of One Stop Centres (OSCs) and 
women helpline schemes and important proposals received under Nirbhaya Fund.  
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION

Development has been Rs.22094.67 crore which is Rs.4686.55 crore more than the budget 
allocations and Rs.4454.32 crore more than revised allocations of the year 2016-17.   The budget 
allocation of the Ministry for the year 2017-18 shows an overall increase of 21.22 and 20.17 per 
cent respectively when compared with the budget and revised allocations of 2016-17.  A

2.4 The Committee also notes that for the child development  schemes there is an

development goal for any society if it wishes to be a developed and equal society.  This goa l 
requires gender equality which in turn needs critical policy steps in favour of women.  Indian 
women have traditionally been vulnerable and marginalized section in the society.  This is 
the reason that the constitution of India not only prohibits discrimination on the grounds of 
sex but also permits positive discrimination in favour of women.  Seen in this context, the 
formulation and implementation of women centric schemes acquires utmost importance.  It  
is the implementation part of the schemes that suffers due to lack of funds.  Therefore, it is  
Committee’s concerted opinion th at sufficient funds should be provided for the women 
welfare schemes as well if the objective of socio-economic development of women  is to be 
achieved.  Further, the Committee feels that there is a need to universalize women w elfare 
schemes also so as to ensure their participation in social, economic and political decision 
making process.

feels that there should be optimum utilization of funds under each of the schemes of t he Ministry if 
the desired goals of various schemes were to be achieved. Since all the schemes of the Ministry are 
meant for the development and welfare of children and women, it is of utmost impor tance that 
allocated funds are utilized optimally to cover targeted beneficiaries.  The Commi ttee accordingly, 

recommends that the factors responsible for under utilization of funds be identifi ed and remedial 
action taken in a time bound manner.  The Committee further desires that a status note be furnished 
on the schemes where utilization of funds has been abysmally low in respect of the budget allocations. 
2.7 The Committee also observes that under-achievement of financial targets in a number 
of schemes is indicative of the fact that physical targets of those schemes remained under-
achieved as well.  The Committee believes that the schemes of children and wom en are of 
vital importance and under-achievement of these schemes would necessarily mean that the 
benefits of the schemes have not reached  the targeted beneficiaries  or they have been denied 
the benefits of welfare schemes.   In this context, the Committee feels that problems faced in 
the achievements of both financial and physical targets should be identified and addr essed 
for efficacious implementation of the schemes.  The Ministry should also take up the matt er 
of under-achievement with the concerned State Governments/UTs for resolving constraints. 
III INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES  (ICDS) SCHEME 
3.1 The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme is one of the flagship 
programmes of the Government of India and represents one of the world’s largest and unique 
programmes for early childhood care and development.  The beneficiaries under the scheme are 
children in the age group of 0-6 years, pregnant women and lactating mothers.  The ICDS Sc heme 
offers a package of six services, viz, : 
(i) supplementary nutrition; 
(ii) pre-school non-formal education; 
(iii) nutrition and health education; 
(iv) immunization; 
(v) health check-up; and 
(vi) referral services. 
  
Immunization, health check-up and referral services are related to health and are provided 
by the Department of Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of Health and Family W elfare through 
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and health system.  Convergence is one of the key 
features of the ICDS Scheme for better governance in the delivery of the scheme.  This 
convergence is inbuilt in the scheme which provides a platform in the form of Anganwadi Centres 
for providing  all services under the scheme.  The ICDS scheme has been gradually universali zed 
and currently 7076 projects and 14 lakh Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) have been approved.  This 
also includes a provision of 20,000 AWCs ‘on demand’.  As on 30. 9.2016, out of 14 lakh 
approved AWCs about 13.49 lakh AWCs are operational. 

3.2 The Committee was given to understand that in order to address various programmatic, 
management and institutional gaps and to meet administrative and operational challenges, th e 
Government had approved the strengthening and restructuring of ICDS Scheme with an allocation 
of Rs.1,23,580 crore during the 12 th Five Year Plan.  The budget allocation and expenditure under 
the ICDS Scheme during the 12 th Five Year Plan and the budget allocation of 2017-18 is as shown

of Rs. 14,000 crore was even less than the total expenditure of Rs. 15438.93 crore in the previous

3.4 The Ministry listed the   following problem areas in the implementation of Integrated 
Development Child Services (ICDS) Scheme due to fund shortage:- 
- The Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) while considering continuation of ICDS 
scheme during the Fourteen Finance Commission (FFC) period i.e. 2017-18 to 2019-20 has 
recommended  payment of entire salary of regular field staff by the States/UTs and the 
construction of AWC buildings from sources other than ICDS.  No fund has bee n 
earmarked for this purpose.  These are ongoing components and their discontinuation 
would adversely affect  the scheme. 

- Construction of 4 lakh AWCs is to be done through convergence with MGNREGA with 
their contribution of Rs.5 lakh per unit and Rs. 2 lakh contributed  by MWCD.  
Discontinuation   of this activity will stop the units  already under construction  and further 
sanction of units will be hampered.  It is needless to say that provision of pucca building is 
pre-requisite  for delivery of child related services. 
- Ministry of WCD has requested Ministry of Finance  to allocate  additional funds of Rs. 
12612 crore for (FFC) period 2017-18 to 2019-20 for paying salary to the regular  field 
level staff and for construction of AWC buildings. 
- There  are 2.86 lakh AWC government  owned buildings without toilet facilities and 1.25 
lakh government owned buildings  without drinking water facility.  Provision of funds for 
providing these services is very essential. 
- Ministry has requested the Government to provide a supplementary grant of Rs. 896.40 
crore for the current financial year 2016-17 as the allocated amount is not sufficient to meet 
the cost. 
3.5 The Committee while taking note of the above problems observes  that ICDS scheme 
is one of the biggest and most unique scheme of the Ministry aimed at improving the 
nutritional and health status of children in the age group of 0-6 years and laying the 
foundation of their proper psychological, physical and social development.  It is of utmost  
importance that adequate funds  should be provided under the scheme to cov er all the 
targeted beneficiaries who are children in 0-6 years of age, pregnant women an d lactating 
mothers.    The  Committee notes that  the Ministry  has got around 15 per ce nt less 
allocation in BE 2017-18 than their projected demand . It is Committee’s concerted view that 
shortage of fund should not hamper the proper implementation of the scheme  and  the 
Committee desires the Ministry to ensure adequate funds for proper implemen tation of the 
ICDS Scheme.

sanctioned AWCs operational, it was informed that the Ministry continuously moni tors the implementation 
of ICDS scheme including the operationalization of AWCs through reports, returns, field visits and review 
meetings  at the national level.  ICDS being a self selecting scheme, states/UTs have been advised to 
operationalize the pending ICDS projects and Anganwadi centres (AWCs) immediately.  As for the reasons 
for delay it was informed that they were largely administrative, legal and court  cases as reported by the 
States/UTs.  The Committee feels that the constraints in making the sanctioned AWCs operational 
need to be tackled and remedial steps taken in an urgent manner as AWCs are the platform fro m 
where ICDS Services are rendered to the beneficiaries.

Supplementary Nutrition Programme (SNP) 
3.11 Supplementary Nutrition is one of the six services being delivered at AWCs under the 
ICDS scheme. Provision of supplementary nutrition is primarily made to bridge the gap between 
Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) and the Average Daily Intake (ADI) of children and 
pregnant and lactating women. Under the revised nutritional and feeding norms which have been 
made effective from February 2009, State Governments/UTs have been directed to provide 300 
days of supplementary food to the beneficiaries in a year which would entail giving more than one 

meal to the children from 3-6 years who come to AWCs. This includes morning snacks in the form 
of milk/banana/egg/seasonal fruits/micro-nutrient fortified food followed by a Hot Cooked Meal. 
For children below 3 years of age and pregnant and lactating mothers, age appropriate Take Home 
Rations (THRs) in the form of pre-mix/ready-to-eat food are provided. Besides for severely 
underweight children in the age of 6 months to 6 years, additional food items in the form of 
micronutrient fortified food and/or energy dense food as THR have been recommended.

IV INTEGRATED CHILD PROTECTION SCHEME (ICPS) 
4.1 The Integrated Child Protection Scheme was revised in the year 2014-15 and has come into 
effect from 1st April, 2014. Some of the key features of the revised scheme are increased 
maintenance grant for children in homes, from existing Rs.750/- to Rs.2000/- per child per month, 
enhanced cost of construction from existing provision from R600 per sq. Feet to Rs.1000/- per sq. 
Feet, flexibility in the staffing pattern and in service delivery structures, depending on the size and 
need of State/UT, to provide child protection services in a more cost effective manner; and 
flexibility to States to source additional funds from corporate/private donors for any component of 
the Scheme.  
 
4.2  The scheme provides financial support to State Governments/UT Administrations for 
running services for children either themselves or through suitable NGOs. These services include 
(a) Homes of various types for children; (b) Emergency Outreach services through Childline; (c) 
15 Open Shelters for children in need of care and protection in Urban and Semi Urban Areas; (d)  
Family Based Non-Institutional Care through Sponsorship and Foster Care and Adoptions. 
 
4.3 Financial Assistance under the Scheme is also provided for setting up of statutory bodies 
under the Juvenile Justice Act namely; Child Welfare Committees (CWCs) and Juvenile Justice 
Boards (JJBs). As reported by the State Governments/UT Administrations, so far 675 CWCs and 
669 JJBs have been set up across the country.  The budget allocation under the ICPS for the 12 th 
Plan period was Rs. 2350.00 crore.  Against the allocated BE of Rs.400.00 crore for  2016-17, 
amount of Rs.335.58 crore has been released upto 31.12.2016.

number.  The Khoya-Paya portal has been integrated as a citizen corner on the track child portal.

4.9 On a specific query regarding efforts made by the Ministry to strengthen the mechanism 
for monitoring of quality services at the Juvenile Homes so as to prevent abuse or exploitation of 
children, the Ministry submitted that Section 41 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of 
Children) Act, 2015 has made registration of Homes mandatory within six months of the Act 
coming into force. There are stringent penalties in case of non-compliance.  Under Section 8, the 
Juvenile Justice Board is required to conduct at least one inspection visit every month of 
residential facilities for children in conflict with law and recommend action for improvement in 
quality of services to the District Child Protection Unit and the State Government.  Further, under 
Section 54, State Government is required to appoint inspection committees for the State and 
district.  The inspection Committees are required to mandatorily conduct visits to all facilities 

housing children, at least once in three months.  The Act also includes detailed rehabilitation and 
re-integration services that are to be provided to institutions registered under the Act such as 
education, vocational training, skill development, mental health interventions including 
counselling, recreational activities, etc. 
 
4.10 The Committee, while noting the reply of the Ministry would like to reiterate that the 
well meaning laws alone would not make any change at ground level.  There is n o denying 
the fact that the living conditions at most juvenile homes in the country are so worse that 
they could be termed as violation of both human and child rights.   There are persistent 
problems of inadequate space, bathrooms, toilets, cleanliness, lack of recreational activities, 
life skills and vocational training and staff shortage.   
 
4.11 The Committee was  given to understand that the staff attrition rate was very high due to 
low salaries under ICPS scheme.  The Ministry has since enhanced the staff salary norms.  Prior to 
the revision, the lowest salary was of Ayahs, cooks etc at Rs. 2000/- per month, it has been 
enhanced to Rs.6000/- per month.  Similarly, the highest salary of the programme managers has 
been enhanced from Rs. 20,000/- per month to Rs. 35,000/- .  The Committee while noting the 
above reply recommends that the Ministry being the nodal authority for all child-wel fare 
measures has to be pro-active in sensitizing the states/UTs  to strive for improving the living 
conditions of the Juvenile homes as per the mandate of the Juvenile (Care and Protection of 
Children) Act,  2015. 
 
V. BETI BACHAO BETI PADHAO (BBBP) 
5.1 Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (BBBP) was launched by the Prime Minister on 22 nd January, 
2015 at Panipat, Haryana.  BBBP addresses the declining Child Sex Ratio (CSR) and related issues 
of women empowerment over a life-cycle continuum.  It is a tri-ministerial effort of Ministries of 
Women and Child Development, Health and Family Welfare and Human Resource Development.  
The key elements of the scheme include Enforcement of Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic 
Techniques Act (PCPNDT), nation-wide awareness and advocacy campaign and multi-sectoral 
action in select 100 districts (low on CSR) in the first phase.  There is a strong emphasis on 
mindset change through training, sensitization, awareness raising and community mobilization.

 The scheme is well received in the selected 100 districts and seeing the criticality of the 
CSR issue, it has been expanded  in additional  61 districts covering 11 States/UTs. 
 
5.2 The Ministry informed the Committee about the achievements of BBBP scheme as under: 
- since its inception, the scheme has resulted in hundreds  of local level innovative initiatives 
to promote the girl child; 
- the preliminary reports of 100 districts  indicate that for the time period between April-
March, 2014-15 & 2015-16, an increasing trend in Sex Ratio at Birth (SRB) is visibile in 
58 BBBP districts; 
- 69 districts have reported progress  in the first trimester registration, against the reported 
ANC registrations and status of institutional deliveries have improved in 80 districts; 
- the gir ls’ enrolment in secondary education has increased to 80.67  per cent  as per the 
Unified District Information System for Education in 2015-16 against 76 per cent in 2013-
14. 
- construction of girls’ toilets in every school in selected 100 low CSR district s (Phase-I) has 
been completed. 
 
5.3 The Committee notes that the Child Sex Ratio (CSR), an indicator of gender discrimination 
towards girl child stands at 918 girls per 1000 boys in the age group of 0-6 years, much lower than 
the figure of 927 in 2001 Census.  The unabated decline in CSR since 1961 is a matter of grav e 
concern as it reflects the low status of women in our society and indicates her disempowerment.  
There are many areas/pockets in the country where the child sex ratio has been below the nati onal 
average or declining and such areas/pockets  have been expanding due to various socio-economic 
factors.  As per the information available  to the Committee by  the Ministry, out of 640 districts 
across the country, 429 districts have declining CSR.  The Committee feels that the declining 
CSR is a major social problem requiring urgent remedial action before it is too late.   
Accordingly, the Committee recommends  that the Ministry should make concerted efforts to 
check this declining CSR in a mission mode manner and also to put more aggre ssiveness, 
energy and resources to reverse this trend.

VI SCHEME FOR ADOLESCENT GIRLS  
6.1 The scheme for Adolescent Girls formerly, the Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for empowerment of 
adolescent girls - SABLA introduced on a pilot basis in August, 2010 and is presently operational 
in 205 selected districts across the country.  SABLA was aims at all-round development of 
adolescent girls (AGs) of 11-18 years (with a focus on all out-of-school AGs) by making them 
'self-reliant' by improving their health and nutrition status, promoting awareness about health, 
hygiene, nutrition, Adolescent Reproductive and Sexual Health (ARSH), family and child care and 
facilitating access to learning about public services through various interventions such as guidance 
and counselling as well as Vocational Training.  It also aims towards mainstreaming 'out of school 
AGs' into formal/non-formal education.  The scheme has two major components Nutrition and 
Non Nutrition Component. 
 
6.2 Under the nutrition component of the scheme, the out of school adolescent girls in the age 
group of 11-14 years and all the girls in the age group of 14-18 years attending Anganwadi C enres 
are provided  supplementary nutrition (@ Rs. 5/- per beneficiary per day for 300 days in a ye ar) in 

the form of Take Home Ration or that cooked meals.  Under the non-nutrition component, out of 
school adolescent girls of 11-18 years are being provided services including – Iron and Folic Acid 
(IFA) supplementation, health check-up and referral services, nutrition and health education, 
counselling/guidance  on family welfare, Adolescent Reproductive and Sexual Health, life skill 
education, guidance on accessing  public services and vocational training (only 16-18 years of 
adolescent girls).  The scheme also aims at mainstreaming  out of school AGs to school system.  
Nearly one crore beneficiaries are covered  for nutrition annually under the scheme.

VIII HOSTELS FOR WORKING WOMEN 
8.1 Under the Scheme of Working Women Hostel financial assistance is provided for 
construction/running of Hostel in rented premises for those working women who may be single, 
widowed, divorced,  separated, married or whose husband or immediate family does not reside in 
the same area and for those women who are under training for job.  Provision of day care centre 
for children of the inmates of the Hostel is an important aspect of the scheme.  The scheme has 
been revised in June, 2015.  As per revised guidelines, working women are entitled to hostel 
facilities provided their gross income does not exceed `50,000 consolidated (gross) per month in 
metropolitan cities, or Rs.35,000 consolidated (gross) per month, in any other place.  When the 
income of any working women already residing in a hostel exceeds the prescribed limits, she will 
be required to vacate the hostel within a period of six months of crossing the income limit.  

Implementing Agencies will be provided financial assistance for installing Solar Water Heating 
System/Gyser and providing Washing Machines for the use of inmates of the Hostel. 
8.2 In 1972-73, since its inception, 934 hostels have been sanctioned under the scheme all over 
the country benefitting about 70,139 working women.  The Committee  is given to understand that 
during the last two years and current year 44 new proposals  have been received.  Complete and 
viable proposals recommended by the concerned State Government were considered by the project 
sanctioning committee and 25 new proposals were sanctioned.  The financial progress data of the 
scheme for the years 2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17 show  that there has always  been under 
utilization of funds.

IX SWADHAR GREH 
9.1 The Ministry of Women and Child Development was earlier implementing two schemes i.e 
Swadhar  and Short Stay Homes (SSH) to provide shelter, food , clothing, counselling, training, 
clinical and legal aid with  the aim to rehabilitate women in  difficult circumstances  and to 
provide temporary accommodation, maintenance and rehabilitative services to women  and girls in 
distress.  As effectiveness and positive impact  of the schemes  was similar, therefore, it was 
decided to merge the above the two schemes into a new scheme, namely the Swadhar Greh w.e.f 
01.01.2016.  The Swadhar Greh Scheme  targets women victim of unfortunate  circumstances who 
are in need of institutional  suppot for rehabilitation so that they may lead their life with dignit y.  
The new scheme  envisions setting up of one such home in every district.  Swadhar Greh aims to 
provide temporary residential  accommodation with provision of food, clothing, medical facilities, 
vocational and skill upgradation trainings  for economic  rehabilitation of such women.  The 
scheme is implemented by the State Governments/UT Administrations.  The funding pattern is 
60:40 between Centre and the States excepting for the North-Eastern and Himalayan States where 
it is 90:10.  In case of UT Administrations, 100 per cent funding is born by the Central 
Government.

XI NATIONAL MISSION FOR EMPOWERMENT OF WOMEN (NMEW) 
11.1 The National Mission for Empowerment of Women (NMEW) Scheme was  approved with 
a mandate to strengthen inter-sectoral convergence  of programmes, policies and schemes  for 
women both at the centre and at the State/UT level.  The scheme is meant to strengthen efforts  
through inter-sectoral coordination amongst different ministries and programmes with the Ministry 
of Women and Child Development as the nodal Ministry.  It also endeavours  to facilitate  the 
reach of various services  and programmes of the Central and State Governments to the target 
group  of women.  Training and Capacity building to enhance  and strengthen understanding of 
gender issues  and bridge the gap between knowledge and practice  is the other focus are a of 
NMEW. 
11.2 National Mission for Empowerment of Women (NMEW) was  approved as a centrally 
sponsored  scheme during the terminal year of 11 th Five Year Plan with 100 per cent central 
funding.  Following restructuring of Centrally Sponsored schemes in July, 2013 the scheme was 

revised.  NMEW scheme is now being implemented on the basis of 60:40 centre-state sharing 
except North-Eastern and special category states where the cost sharing ratio is 90:10. 
11.3 On a specific query regarding the achievements of the NMEW scheme, the Ministry has 
informed that the scheme has been able to make progress  towards addressing holistic 
empowerment  of women in terms of bridging gender issues centre-stage  across  different 
States/UTs.  The gender experts engaged  as part of technical support to the Ministry of WCD in 
the fields of Poverty Alleviation, Social Empowerment, Health and Nutrition, Gender Budgeting, 
Gender Rights, Empowerment of Vulnerable and Marginalized Women and Women in Difficult  
Circumstances, Media and Communications etc. are supporting various women centric 
schemes/programs of the government while engaging consistently and continuously with a wide 
range of stakeholders.  The scheme has played an important role towards  enhancing the capacity 
of functionaries through  training and capacity building.  Several consultations at regional level 
have been held with State Governments and civil society organizations to take the discourse on 
gender issues to a wider audience as well as identify key issues that need immediate action.  In 
pursuance to the same, NMEW has been working towards engendering institutions and 
strengthening Gender Focal Points within institutions at various levels including Central 
Ministries, State Governments, Local Self Governments (LSGs) etc. for  enabling these institutions 
to identify and respond to gender issues. Developed participatory tools such as Nari ki Chaupal to 
create open fora to discuss gender issues and sharing   of experience and best practic es.  Nari ki 
Chaupal are being organized on regular basis. 
11.4 The State Resource Centre for Women (SRCW) established  under the respective State 
Government/UT Administrative to facilitate convergence of schemes and programmes meant for 
women has been strengthened by timely disbursement of funds and approval of the State Action 
Plans during Financial Year 2016-17.  SRCWs are functional with dedicated staff in 25 
States/UTs. 
11.5 In order to facilitate convergence of schemes/programs at the ground level and enable 
greater access for women to government schemes/programs and create awareness on gender issues 
Poorna Shakti Kendra (PSK) project was conceived in a pilot mode for selected districts.  The PSK 
project entails setting up of convergence centres at the district, block and Gram Panchayat (GP 
level).  Each centre/Kendra at GP level has two Mahila Gram Samanvyaks (Village Coordinators) 
who act as motivators for the women in the area and are also responsible for providing 

support/facilitation on various issues that affect women's empowerment.  The first pilot project to 
demonstrate convergence of programmes and schemes was launched in District Pali, Rajasthan on 
September, 16, 2011.  NMEW  has released/revalidated  funds for 20 PSK  projects during 2016-
17. 
11.6 The PSK projects have been instrumental in bringing about greater access and awareness 
related to women centric schemes/programs at the village level.  With the learning from this 
project, Village Convergence and Facilitation Service (VCFS) gas been extended to cover 200 
high burden districts in the  country.   VCFS was initially  approved for 100 BBBP districts during 
2015-16 and extended  to additional 61 BBBP districts during  2016-17.

11.8 The Committee observes that the objectives of the National Mission for 
Empowerment of Women Scheme are of vital importance as they aim to empower women 
socially, economically and educationally.  However, the pace of the expenditure  under the

of funds is indicative of the fact that  the benefits  of the scheme  are not reaching the 
targeted  beneficiaries.  The  Committee feels that the Ministry should play a pro -active role 
in achieving the objectives of the scheme by completing the process of putting all the 
necessary structures in place and receipt of viable proposals from the States/UTs.  The 
Committee hopes that the pace of expenditure would pick up in 2017-18 and the allocation  of 
Rs.70.00 crore for the year 2017-18 would be fully utilized. 
 
XII NIRBHAYA SCHEMES 

12.1 As per the guidelines of Ministry of Finance dated 25.3.2015, Ministry of Women and 
Child Development is the nodal authority for appraisal of the schemes/proposals received under 
Nirbhaya Fund.  The proposals as and when received from various Central Ministries/agencies are 
appraised and recommended by an Empowered Committee of officers under Nirbhaya Fund on 
priority.  Apart from this, MWCD is administering two schemes namely, One Stop Centre Scheme 
(OSC) and Universalisation of Women Helpline (WHL) under Nirbhaya Fund. 
One Stop Centre Scheme (OSC) 
12.2 The One Stop Centre Scheme was approved in March, 2015 for setting up of One Stop 
Centre’s  in each State/UT to facilitate access to an integrated range of services including medical 
aid, police assistance, legal aid/case management, psychosocial counselling, temporary support 
services to women affected by violence.  The Scheme is being implemented from 1 st April, 2015.  
Under OSC scheme it has been envisaged to set up one centre in every State/UT in first phase and 
its expansion in another 150 additional locations has been sanctioned in second phase.  So far, 79 
centres have become operational in 25 States/UTs and the remaining centres are in various stages 
of operationalization. The scheme has a total project cost of Rs. 119.69 crore. 
Women Helpline (WHL) 
12.3 The Women Helpline Scheme with a total project cost of Rs.69.49 crore was approved in 
February, 2015 for implementation in 2015-16.  The scheme of Women Helpline is exclusively 
designed to support women affected by violence, both in private and public spaces, including in 
the family, community, workplace etc.  The Women Helpline will provide 24 hour emergency 
response to all women affected by violence both in public and private sphere.  So far, women 
helplines have become operational in 18 States/Union Territories.   For the year 2017-18, the 
physical target is to universalize women helpline in 36 States/UTs.

funds allocated under the schemes are utilized to the full  extent. The Committee stresses the 
need for effective implementation of the schemes. The Committee, however, finds that the 
fund utilization under both the One Stop Centre and Women Helpline schemes has been 
very low.  It is a complete irony that on the one hand, crime against women have been rising 
and on the other, funds allocated to enhance the safety and security of women have remained 
underutilized.  The Committee urges upon the government to ensure that the initiatives 
under the Nirbhaya Fund are translated into reality. 
XIII CENTRAL ADOPTION RESOURCE AUTHORITY (CARA) 
13.1 The Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA), which was an Autonomous Body of 
the Ministry of Women and Child Development, has now become a statutory body as per the 
provisions of Section 68, Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015.  It 
functions as a nodal body at National level on adoption related matters of Indian children.  The 
mandate of CARA is to promote in-country adoptions in coordination with state agencies, regulate 
inter-country adoptions, frame regulations on adoption and to carry out the functions of the of the 
Central Authority under the Hague  Convention on Protection for Children and Co-operation in 
respect of inter-country adoption.  CARA has framed the Adoption Regulations 2017 which have 
been operationalized w.e.f 16th January, 2017.  It has also been informed that adoption procedure 
has further been simplified as it is entirely facilitated through on-line system.  CARA has engaged  
Helpline staff (toll free) to assist all prospective adoptive parents.  One counselling centre at 
CARA is operational and there is a proposal  to extend it to the State and district level to ensure 
that Prospective Adoptive Parents (PAPs) have excess to counselling help. 
13.2 The Committee has been made to understand that the adoption regulations, 2017 have been 
framed keeping in mind the issues and challenges faced by CARA and other  stakeholders 
including the adoption agencies and the prospective adoptive parents (PAPs).  This will further 
strengthen adoption programme in the country by streamlining the adoption process.  

Transparency, early deinstitutionalization of children, informed choices for the parents, ethical 
practices and strictly defined  timelines in the adoption process are the salient aspects of the 
adoption regulations. 
13.3 On a specific query regarding promotion of inter-country adoptions and monitoring 
mechanism to check exploitation of children in inter-country adoptions, the Committee was 
informed  that the adoption regulations 2017 has provisions for placing the children with eligible 
and suitable foreign parents if they are not being placed with domestic parents within the stipulated 
time-frame.  The inter-country adoption procedure has adequate safeguards to protect the interest 
of adopted children and is being undertaken as per the Hague Convention on Inter country 
Adoptions to which India is a signatory.  Various recognized agencies and authorities are involved 
to ensure that such children should be de-institutionalised as early as possible and strict adoption 
protection is in place to check any possible exploitation of children.  The eligibility/suitability of 
the Prospective Adoptive Parents is determined on the basis of their Home Study Report (HSR) 
prepared by professional Social Worker in the country of their residence.   The same are further 
assessed by the concerned Authority Foreign Adoption Agency (AFAA) and their  application is 
approved by the concerned Central Authority.  The applications are initially scrutinized  by the 
screening  Committee  and are examined by the NOC Committee in CARA at later stage.  The  
Court  concerned also looks  into the suitability of the inter-country Prospective Adoptive Parents, 
before issuing  Adoption Order in their favour.

XIV NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN (NCW) 
14.1 The National Commission for Women (NCW) was constituted in 1992 as a statutory body 
under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990 at the  national level to safeguard and 
promote the rights and interests of women.   It has  a wide mandate covering almost all aspect of 
women’s development.  The Commission investigates and examines the legal safeguards provided  
for women under constitution  and other laws  and recommends  to the government, measures for 
their effective implementation.  The Commission also reviews the existing provisions of the 
constitution  and other laws affecting women and recommends amendments to meet any lacunae 
or inadequacies in such laws.  It also looks into complaints and takes suo-motu cognizance  on 
matters  relating to deprivation of women’s  rights.  The Commission takes up studies/research on 
issues of relevance  to women, participates  and advises in the planning process for socio-
economic development of women, evaluates the program made thereof, inspects jails, remand and 
shelter homes etc. where women are kept under custody and seeks remedial action wherever  
necessary. The Commission also focuses on public awareness regarding laws and schemes relating 
to women.

PREFACE

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee, do hereby
present, on its behalf, the Twenty-ninth Report on the University Grants Commission
(Amendment) Bill, 1995.

2. The Bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 2nd June, 1995. It was referred to
the Committee by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, vide Bulletin Part I! dated June 6, 1995, for
examination and report.

3. The Amendment Bill aims at enhancing the penalty for violation of Sections 22 and
23 of the University Grants Commission Act, 1956, by amending Section 24 of the same
Act. The penalty for violation of these sections at present is a maximum fine of. Rs. one
thousand. This is proposed to be enhanced to a minimum punishment of imprisonment of
not less than six months, which may extend to three years, and also a fine of not less than
Rs. one lakh, which may extend to Rs, 10 lakhs. The amendment also provides that the
court may award lesser punishment for reasons to be recorded in the judgement.

4. A Press Release, inviting suggestions from individuals, organisations and institutions
interested in the subject matter of the Bill, was issued. (Annexure-I), 46 memoranda,
containing views, opinions, comments and suggestions, were received by the Committee in
response thereto. (List at Annexure-II).

5. The Committee considered the Bill in two sittings and heard the oral evidence of the
Secretary, Department of Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development and the
Chairman, University Grants Commission, and also of the representative of the Legislative
Department, Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs.

6. The Committee, in its meeting held on August 9, 1995, considered the draft report
on the Bill and adopted the same for presgntation/laying in both the Houses of Parliament.

REPORT

The problem of fake universities awarding unrecognised degrees has been engaging the
attention of the University Grants Commission and the Government of India for the past
few years. A ‘Fake’ university is an institution which is not entitled to call itself a university
or award degrees. According to Section 2(f) of the University Grants Commission Act 1956,
a “University” means, ‘‘a University established or incorporated by or under a Central Act,
a provincial Act or a State Act, and includes any such institution as may, in consultation
with the University concerned, be recognized by the Commission in accordance with the
regulations made in this behalf under this Act.”

2. Thus, any University, which has not been created under an Act of Parliament or of a
state Legislature or has not been granted the status of a deemed university, under section 3
of the University Grants Commission Act 1956, cannot call itself a University or award
degrees. Since the penalty available in the Act to check the growth of ‘fake’ universities/
institutions is only Rs. 1,000 (maximum), a large number of fake institutions/organisations’
have been operating in various parts of the country, duping the gullible students.

3. As per the information furnished by the University Grants Commission, there are, at
present, 27 such institutions, which style themselves as ‘universities’ and award degree
illegally. A list of such institutions is given at ANNEXURE-III.

4. The Committee on Petitions (VIII Lok Sabha), in its 9th Report, had dealt with this
subject while discussing the question of recognition of ‘Maithili University’ in the year, 1989
and made the following two important recommendations in this regard for implementation
by the Government:

(i) The machinery for watching implementation of the provisions of the UGC Act
may be streamlined and made more effective and purposeful. If need be, the
provisions of UGC Act miay be suitably amended so that there is a self-working
system aimed at checking the activities of institutions/organisations which tend to
exploit the gullible youth by resorting to illegal methods;

(ii) The penalty envisaged in Section 24 appears to be too mild. In order that it may
have a deterrent effect, it may be suitably enhanced and even imprisonment may
be provided for by amending the relevant Section of the Act.

5. The Deptt. of Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development, had introduced
in the Rajya Sabha on 11.12.1991, a Bill titled ‘the University Grants Commission
(Amendment) Bill, 1991, with the object of:—

(a) empowering the UGC to specify, by regulations, the terms and conditions of
service, including the scales of pay of the Officers/employees and teachers of
central universities; and

(b) providing for deterrent punishment for persons establishing and running fake
universities.

6. Since there were sharp reactions from the teaching and non-teaching employees of
Central Universities, the Government decided to refer the Bill to the University Grants
Commission for examination and report. The University Grants Commission constituted a

(iii) In Section 24 of the principal Act, for the words ‘which may extend to Rs. 1,000

7. In view of the ‘above recommendations, the University Grants Commission

Chairman, Rajya Sabha, for examination and repoft.

8. Keeping in view the concern of the Government and the general public over the
mushrooming of self-styled ‘universities’ functioning in different parts of the country, the
Committee has immediately taken up considesation of the bill and issued a Press
Communique as well as an advertisement, in leading newspapers inviting the views/

examination and comments. The Committee wishes to place on record its appreciation of the
promptness with which the .Ministry sent its comments/replies on the representations,
although the time given to it was very short. At the same time, the Committee is at a loss to
understand why, after so many years during which there has been no effective law against
fake universities, the Ministry has come up with an Amendment Bill which does not take
into account the first recommendation of the Committee on Petitions and remains limited to
a very narrow scope.

comprehensive list of all such fake universities/institutions and publish them for the
information of the general public so that innocent youth do not fall prey to the activities of
these so-called universities/institutions.

11. The Committee is pained to note that even today many institutions are taking undue
advantage of the lacuna in the Act. There are many institutions which get themselves
registered under the Societies Registration Act and start using the title of a ‘University
without even informing the University Grants Commission

12. Some institutions have been associating the word ‘Vidyapeeth’ in the nomenclature
of the institute to create an impression of ‘University’ in the minds of the general. public.
The Chairman, University Grants Commission, informed the Committee that the definition
of the ‘University’. in the Hindi version of the Act does not mention the: word and it
mentions only “Vishwavidyalaya”, Therefore, action against the institutions using the ward
‘Vidyapeeth’ in their nomenclature cannot be taken within the ambit of the definition of the
‘University’ contained in Section 2(f) of the Act. Unless a suitable amendment is carried out
in the definition of the word ‘University’, as given in the Act, the Government would not be
able to restrain the unscrupulous elements from take advantage of the ambiguity prevailing
in the existing Act. This is more so because there are some reputed institutions with the
name of ‘Vidyapeeth’ which are either Universities or Deemed-Universities e.g ‘Gujarat
Vidyapeeth’, ‘Kashi Vidyapeeth’ and ‘the Lal ‘Bahadur Shastri Kendriya Sanskrit
Vidyapeeth’, etc. The unsuspecting student community falls prey and becomes a victim of
the fake universities using the word ‘Vidyapeeth’ after their names. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that a separate Schedule may be annexed to the Aét
mentioning the words ‘University’, ‘Vishwavidyalaya’, and such other words as may be used
in other regional languages so as to cover them under the definition of ‘University’, as
contained in the Section 2(f of the Act

13, As mentioned earlier, the Committee on Petitions (VIII Lok Sabha), in its 9th
Report given in the year 1989, had made two important recommendations. Of the two
recoramendations, the Department of Education and the University Grants Commission
have 109 brought forward amendmént to Section 24 of the University Grants Commission
Act, only proposing to enhance the penalty for violation of Sections 22 and 23 of the Act.
The officials of the Ministry and the University Grants Commission could not come out with
any satisfactory explanation as to why no action has so far been taken on the first
recommendation of the Committee on Petitions regarding creation of a self-working system,
which was equally important for arresting the activities and the growth of fake institutions/
organisations mushrooming in the country. The Committee strongly feels that unless a self-
working system within the University Grants Commission is created to act as a vigilance
machinery/cell and also to monitor the activities of such institutions, the objective sought to
be achieved by the present Amendment will not be accomplished in its true spirit. Therefore,
the Committee feels that there is an urgent need to bring in a more comprehensive
amendment so as to encompass the various facets of the problem within the ambit of the law
to arrest the nefarious activities of these institutions/organisations.

14. At present, neither the University Grants Commission nor the Deptt. of Education
owns the responsibility for taking action against the fake institutions coming to their notice
The University Grants Commission feels that the State Government machinery will take
cognizance of the offence suo motu. The State Government machinery, particularly the
police authorities, are already preoccupied with other problems and seldom take cognizance
of these offences. Therefore, neither the University Grants Commission nor the State
Government takes action against these institutions. It is only when a complaint is made,



4

either to the Deptt. of Education or the University Grants Commission, some kind of action
is initiated, which is neither effective nor considered to be deterrent. The University Grants
Commission often writes to the State Governments to take action against such institutions,
Very rarely, prosecutions are launched against these institutions and the University Grants
Commission officials could not cite any case where prosecution launched had resulted in
conviction of the persons responsible for these illegal activities. In most of the cases, we find
that the legal process continues for years and the ‘fake’ universities continue to flourish in
the meantime. The Committee, therefore, feels that there should be some mechanism or
machinery to find out the existence of these institutions and the Act should specify the
authorities responsible to take action against these institutions. The authorities, so specified in
the Act, should be made accountable and responsible for taking action in these matters. In
case these authorities failed to act at the appropriate time, there should be provision for
suitable action against them, as their in action also contributes to the growth and rise of these
fake institutions ruining the careers of thousands of youth,

15. The University Grants Commission/Deptt. of Education could not cite cases
wherein they had acted effectively and launched prosecution proceedings against these
institutions. Even in the cases where prosecutions have been launched, such as in the case of
“Maithili University’ the State Government has failed to pursue the matters with the court
vigoruosly, resulting in the continued existence of these institutions. For example, a case is
reported to have been registered against ‘Maithili’ University’. The self-styled University has
filed a suit against the University Grants Commission in the court of First Munsif,
Darbhanga. The counter affidavit was filed on behalf of the University Grants Commission
and the case was fixed for hearing for 24th April, 1992. The University Grants Commission
or the Deptt. of Education does not know the present fate of the case. Similar is the
position in respect of complaints against Mahila Gram Vidyapeeth/Vishwavidyalaya, Paryag,
Allahabad; Uttar Pradesh Vishwavidyalaya, Kosi Kalan, Mathura (U.P.); DDB Sanskrit
University, Puthur, Trichi (Tamil Nadu) and Testator Research University, Bodinay-Kanur
(Tamil Nadu). These are only a few illustrations of the laxity shown by the University
Grants Commission and the Deptt. of Education in tackling this problem. The Committee,
therefore, recommends creation of a separate cell in the University Grants Commission to
follow-up such cases in courts and with the State Governments. Additional funds should be
made ayailable to the UGC for this purpose.

16. On being asked as to how the University Grants Commission will ensure the closure
of these fake institutions even after the enhancement of the penalty proposed in the present
Amendment Bill, neither the University Grants Commission nor the Deptt. of Education
could come out with any plausible explanation. This means that even after this Amendment
Bill is passed by the Parliament, these institutes will continue to operate despite their
conviction by the courts. The Committee is very much disturbed over this prospect and

ould be a provision in the Act to order closure of these fake

oon as their existence comes to the notice of the authorities. The
onus in that event, will be on the institution concerned to prove its bonafides and legitimacy.
The Committee feels that besides taking penal action, including imposition of fine, closure of
these institutions is very important as otherwise the very purpose of bringing this Amendment
gets defeated. There should also be a provision for confiscation/seizure of the documents,
connected with the running of these institutions, at the time of their closure and confiscation
of properties and assets in case of failure to pay the fine imposed by the court.

17. At present, the so-called ‘fake’ universities/institutions have been liberally giving
advertisements in newspapers tempting the unsuspecting youth of the country to join their



5

institutes for obtaining degrees/diplomas very easily. There is no check by the University
Grants Commission or the Government on such advertisements. Even the newspapers do not
observe any restraint on publishing such advertisements even when they are aware of their
dubious character. Since these advertisements are meant to facilitate the illegal activities of
these institutions, their publication in the newspapers should be banned. The University
Grants Commission and the Deptt. of Education should take up the matter with the Press
Council of India and the Editors Guild, etc. to finalise the modalities for excercising restraint
by newspapers on the publication of such advertisements. The Press cannot shy away from
their social responsibility in this regard, The recognised Universities, while advertising about
their courses, should invariably mention in ‘their advertisements that they are
U.G.C.—recognised universities, so that advertisements relating to the fake universities can
easily be identified by the public.

18. on being asked as to why the Government has made provision in the proposed
Amendment to section 24 of the University Grants Commission Act, giving powers to the
courts to reduce the penalities, as well as imprisonment, for reasons to be recorded in the
judgement, the officials of the Ministry/University Grants Commission stated that this has
been done on the advice of the Union Law Ministry. The representatives of the Ministry of
Law, Justice and Company Affairs. Legislative Deptt. informed that this has been done
keeping in view the legislative practice in vogue at present in such cases. When the
Committee asked as to why the Law Ministry was so kind to the criminals who are bent
upon ruining the careers of the gullible youth, the representative of the Law Ministry could
not come out with any satisfactory reply and agreed that the proviso could be dropped, The
Committee feels that dropping of the proviso is essential if the objectives of the proposed
Amendment are to be achieved.

19. The Committee recommends the Bill for being passed with the modifcation/
recommendations suggested in the preceding paragraphs.

Press Release

The University Grants Commission (Amendment) Bill, 1995, as introduced in the Rajya
Sabha on the 2nd June, 1995, has been referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Human Resource Development, headed by Shri P. Upendra, M.P., for examination and
report. :

2. The Bill proposes to deal with the problem of ‘fake’ ‘universities (i.e. those
universities which are not established under the act of Parliament or a State Legislature or
not granted “deemed to be university” status) by enhancing penalty provision for running
such universities and awarding degrees. The penalty for this at present, is a maximum of Rs,
1,000 under Section 24 of the UGC Act, 1956

3. In view of a large number of ‘fake’ universities operating and duping students all over
the country, the Bill seeks to amend Section 24 of the UGC Act, 1956, to provide that who-
soever contravenes the provisions of Sections 22 and 23 of the said Act shall be liable to be
punished with imprisonment for a term not less than six months which may extend to three
years and would be liable to a fine of Rs. one lakh which may extend to Rs. Ten lakhs. It
further seeks to provide that the Court may, however, award a lesser punishment for reasons
to be recorded in writing

4. The Committee seeks written mefnoranda containing views/suggestions from
individuals, organisations/institutions, etc. interested in the subject matter of the Bill
Accordingly, all those interested are requested to send their views latest by 31st July, 1995,
to Shri N.K. Singh, Deputy Director (HRD), Rajya Sabha Secretariat, Parliament House
Annexe (Room No, 228), New Delhi.

5. Copies of the Bill can be obtained on requisition from the address given above.
